### Spike

Question: What is the consumed HTTP resiliency design that Ikanos should implement, now that the engine targets the current spec (`1.0.0-beta8`) and the MCP adapter speaks protocol `2026-07-28`, and how should #384 be split into implementation stories?

Time-box: 3 days

### Context

#384 is the umbrella for declarative resiliency on consumed HTTP adapters. It requires being split into implementation sub-stories before any implementation starts, and that split cannot be done reliably today:

- The engineering design note that drives this work (tracked internally) was last reviewed against `1.0.0-alpha3`. It predates the move of the MCP adapter to protocol `2026-07-28` (stateless core).
- #384 and that design note diverge on fundamentals: the block name (`resiliency` vs `resilience`), the override levels (API / resource / operation vs control port / namespace / operation), the field names (`attempts`, `duration` vs `maxAttempts`, `timeoutMs`, plus per-attempt `transport` timeouts), and the scope (all seven patterns at once vs retry, time limiter and transport first). The design note also separates resilience primitives (retry, time limiter, transport) from resolution policies (mock, failover, cache), which #384 mixes together.
- The schema and the engine carry no resiliency construct today: `HttpClientAdapter` builds a plain client with no configurable timeout.

The stateless MCP core raises questions the design must answer before stories can be written:

- Which policies are per-call (retry, time limiter, transport) and which keep cross-request state (circuit breaker, rate limiter, bulkhead, cache), and where that state lives in a horizontally scaled deployment.
- How a retry loop reacts when the MCP client cancels the request.
- How a structured outbound failure (classification, attempt count, last status) is projected on each exposed adapter (MCP tool error, REST status code).
- Whether retry eligibility derives from the existing `semantics.idempotent` declaration rather than from the HTTP method.
- Where the boundary lies between a long time limiter and long-running asynchronous execution.

Everything downstream (schema, engine, rules, observability, resolution policies) depends on these answers. This spike produces them; implementation stories are filed afterwards, under #384.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The engineering design note is revised against `1.0.0-beta8` and MCP `2026-07-28`, and synchronized with its internal documentation page.
- [ ] The divergences are settled: block name, override levels, separation between resilience and resolution, cross-request state model, cancellation, error surface, idempotence. Each policy (retry, time limiter, transport, circuit breaker, rate limiter, bulkhead, cache, fallback / failover, mock) is classified as in scope, deferred, or out of scope.
- [ ] A plan lists the implementation sub-stories with their order and dependencies.
- [ ] The sub-stories are filed as sub-issues of #384.
- [ ] The acceptance criteria of #384 are rewritten from that plan.

### Indicative roadmap (to be confirmed or changed by this spike)

| Phase | Goal | Indicative content |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Realignment | This spike | Design revision, decisions, split |
| 2. Schema foundation | Make the configuration declarable | Resilience block (retry, time limiter, transport) on consumed HTTP, field-by-field override, spec model |
| 3. Engine mechanics | Apply it at runtime | Per-attempt transport timeouts, retry loop (backoff, jitter, `Retry-After`, global budget), structured failure per adapter, cancellation |
| 4. Guard-rails | Constrain and observe | Polychro rules, OpenTelemetry span events, documentation |
| 5. Resolution | Declarative mock, failover, cache | `scenarios`, `resolution` block, OpenAPI examples import |
| 6. Stateful policies and runtime control | Cross-request state, hot switching | Circuit breaker, rate limiter, bulkhead; control-port policy switching |
title: Spike: realign consumed HTTP resiliency design with beta8 and MCP 2026-07-28, and split #384

body:
# Spec: Template Dashboard API

## Problem Statement

A developer starting a new authenticated dashboard app has to hand-assemble the same backend every time: registration and login with tokens, a two-role user model, a task board with filtering/sorting/pagination, and password handling. There is no single, contract-first FastAPI implementation to copy.

## Solution

Implement the **Template Dashboard API** as a FastAPI service that conforms exactly to the OpenAPI contract in `docs/openapi.yaml`. The service exposes versioned JSON APIs under `/api/v1`, generates its OpenAPI schema from the code, and keeps it in sync with the contract that drives the frontend MSW/TypeScript layer. It is a single-tenant dashboard: one user pool, one task board, two fixed roles (`admin`, `member`).

## User Stories

### Authentication

1. As a visitor, I want to register with a name, email, and password, so that I can get an account.
2. As a visitor, I want my email to be treated case-insensitively (lowercased) at registration, so that `Alice@X.com` and `alice@x.com` are the same account.
3. As a visitor, I want a clear 409 when my email is already taken, so that I know to log in instead.
4. As a visitor, I want registration to return access and refresh tokens plus my user, so that I'm signed in immediately.
5. As a visitor, I want to log in with email and password, so that I can start a session.
6. As a visitor, I want a 401 on a wrong email or password, so that failed logins are indistinguishable but rejected.
7. As an authenticated user, I want to exchange my refresh token for a new access token, so that I stay signed in without re-entering my password.
8. As an authenticated user, I want refresh to rotate the refresh token (and reject reuse of a stale one), so that a stolen refresh token is detected.
9. As an authenticated user, I want logout to revoke my session, so that the refresh token stops working.
10. As a registrant, I want my account created with the `member` role, so that only admins grant elevated access.

### Users & roles

11. As an authenticated user, I want to fetch my own profile (`GET /users/me`), so that the client can rehydrate my session without a full login.
12. As a member, I want to list all users in the workspace, so that I can pick an assignee for a task.
13. As an admin, I want to list all users with pagination, so that the user management screen scales.
14. As an admin, I want to change another user's role between `admin` and `member`, so that I can grant or revoke admin access.
15. As an admin, I want a guard that prevents demoting or deleting the last admin, so that the workspace can never be left admin-less.
16. As an admin, I want to delete a user, so that I can remove someone from the workspace.
17. As an admin, I want deleting a user to leave their tasks unassigned (not delete them), so that no work is silently lost.
18. As an admin, I want to be unable to delete my own account, so that deletion always goes through another admin.
19. As an admin, I want to create the first admin via a deterministic seed (env var), so that a fresh deploy is not locked out.

### Tasks — creation & editing

20. As an authenticated user, I want to create a task with just a title, so that I can capture work quickly.
21. As an authenticated user, I want to create a task with optional description, status, priority, assignee, and due date, so that I can capture full detail up front.
22. As an authenticated user, I want a new task to default to `todo`, so that tasks don't appear in arbitrary states.
23. As an authenticated user, I want to be able to create a task directly in `in-progress` or `blocked`, but not `done`, so that `done` is only ever reached by a transition.
24. As a member, I want to edit a task I am assigned to, so that I can keep my work current.
25. As a member, I want to be forbidden (403) from editing a task assigned to someone else, so that tasks are owned by their assignee.
26. As a member, I want to reassign or unassign my own tasks, so that I can hand work off.
27. As a member, I want to be unable to acquire someone else's task by setting its assignee to myself, so that self-assignment can't bypass ownership.
28. As an admin, I want to edit or reassign any task, so that I can keep the board correct.
29. As an authenticated user, I want to update a single field without touching others, so that partial updates are safe.
30. As an authenticated user, I want an explicit `null` to clear an optional field (unassign, clear due date), so that clearing is unambiguous.
31. As an authenticated user, I want to move a task through `todo → in-progress → done`, so that status reflects real progress.
32. As an authenticated user, I want to mark a task `blocked` from `todo` or `in-progress`, so that I can flag a dependency.
33. As an authenticated user, I want unblocking a task to return it to its prior state, so that the pause is reversible.
34. As a member, I want to delete a task I am assigned to, so that I can remove my own work.
35. As a member, I want to be forbidden (403) from deleting someone else's task, so that ownership is respected.
36. As an authenticated user, I want to fetch a single task by id, so that the client can deep-link to it.
37. As an authenticated user, I want a 404 for a task id that doesn't exist, so that missing resources are clear.

### Tasks — listing, filtering, sorting, pagination

38. As an authenticated user, I want to list all tasks, so that I can see the whole board.
39. As an authenticated user, I want to filter tasks by a case-insensitive substring on the title (`q`), so that I can search.
40. As an authenticated user, I want to filter by status, so that I can see only what's `todo`, `in-progress`, `done`, or `blocked`.
41. As an authenticated user, I want to filter by priority, so that I can triage by importance.
42. As an authenticated user, I want to filter by assignee (or the literal `unassigned`), so that I can see a person's workload.
43. As an authenticated user, I want to filter by due-date range (`dueDate_gte`/`dueDate_lte`), so that I can see what's due soon.
44. As an authenticated user, I want to paginate with `_start`/`_end`, so that I don't fetch the whole board at once.
45. As an authenticated user, I want an `x-total-count` header with the total matching count, so that the client can render "N of M".
46. As an authenticated user, I want to sort by `title`, `status`, `priority`, or `dueDate`, so that I can order the board my way.
47. As an authenticated user, I want `asc`/`desc` control, so that sorting direction is explicit.
48. As an authenticated user, I want enum fields (`status`, `priority`) to sort in their declared order, so that sorting is meaningful rather than alphabetical.

### Bulk update

49. As an authenticated user, I want to update status, priority, and/or assignee across many tasks in one request, so that I can batch triage.
50. As a member, I want bulk update to apply only to my own tasks and report per-id failures for the rest, so that a mixed batch is safe and transparent.
51. As an authenticated user, I want a bulk response reporting the count updated and the per-id failures, so that I can act on what didn't apply.

### Password

52. As an authenticated user, I want to update my password by providing my current password, so that I can rotate credentials.
53. As an authenticated user, I want a wrong current password to be rejected (400), so that only the account holder can change it.
54. As an authenticated user, I want changing my password to revoke all my other sessions, so that a leaked password locks out other devices.

### Cross-cutting

55. As an API consumer, I want every error as an RFC 9457 problem detail (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`) with a stable `code`, so that clients can branch on the machine-readable code.
56. As an API consumer, I want a stable, documented set of `code` values, so that I can rely on them.
57. As an operator, I want login/register/refresh rate-limited, so that brute-force is slowed.
58. As an operator, I want the OpenAPI schema generated from the code and diffed against the contract, so that drift is caught in CI.

## Implementation Decisions

### Stack

- FastAPI + Python, async endpoints and async database access.
- SQLAlchemy 2.0 async ORM with Alembic migrations.
- Pydantic v2 schemas for request/response validation and serialization.
- PostgreSQL in production; SQLite for local development and tests.
- Argon2id password hashing, minimum 8 characters, no forced character-class rules.
- UUID v4 string identifiers for users and tasks.

### Contract & conventions

- The OpenAPI spec is the single source of truth; the app's generated schema must match `docs/openapi.yaml`.
- Base path `/api/v1`.
- Pagination is `_start`/`_end` with an `x-total-count` response header; the same convention applies to both `GET /tasks` and `GET /users`.
- Sorting: `_sort` + `_order` (`asc` default). Enum fields sort in their declared spec order — `status`: `todo, in-progress, done, blocked`; `priority`: `low, medium, high`.
- PATCH semantics: omitted field = unchanged; explicit `null` = clear.
- Error envelope is RFC 9457: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, plus a stable `code`. Fixed `code` set: `validation_error`, `unauthorized`, `forbidden`, `not_found`, `conflict`, `too_many_requests`, `internal_error`.

### Domain model

- **Single tenant**: one shared workspace, no organization/team boundary.
- **Two fixed roles**: `admin` and `member`, with rules hardcoded per role — no permission/ACL system.
- **User**: identified by a unique, case-insensitive email (lowercased). Lifecycle is register → role change → hard delete; no status/soft-disable.
- **Task**: has `title` (required), optional `description`/`priority`/`dueDate`/`assigneeId`, a `status`, and `createdAt`/`updatedAt`. `assigneeId` may be `null` (unassigned).
- **Ownership = assignment**: a member may update or delete only tasks assigned to them, and may change the assignee only on a task they already own (no self-assignment of others' tasks). Admins may act on any task.
- **Status machine** (from decisions, not a code prototype):

```
todo → in-progress → done
blocked: entered from todo or in-progress; clearing returns to the prior state
never born done (reject status=done on create)
```

### Authorization rules

- Self-registration always produces a `member`; the first admin is seeded via an env var (e.g. `ADMIN_EMAIL`), not by "first user is admin".
- `PATCH /users/{id}/role` and `DELETE /users/{id}` are admin-only.
- Demoting or deleting the last admin is blocked; an admin cannot delete their own account.
- `GET /users` and `GET /users/me` are available to any authenticated user.
- Task mutation (update/delete) is allowed for the assignee, or any admin; otherwise 403.
- Deleting a user sets their tasks' `assigneeId` to `null`.

### Auth & session model

- Access token: JWT bearer, 15-minute lifetime, carries the session identifier.
- Refresh token: stateful, stored server-side in a session record; 30-day lifetime, sliding on rotation; rotated on every refresh (single-use — presenting a stale token revokes the whole session).
- `POST /auth/refresh` returns both a new `accessToken` and a new `refreshToken`.
- `POST /auth/logout` revokes the session identified by the access token's session identifier.
- Password change revokes every other session but keeps the current one.
- Email normalization: lowercase + trim before uniqueness check; duplicate → 409.

## Testing Decisions

- **What makes a good test**: assert only on external behavior — HTTP status, response headers (e.g. `x-total-count`), and JSON body shape/values. Never assert on implementation details (queries, internal call order, table names).
- **The single seam**: the HTTP boundary. Drive the ASGI app through `httpx`/Starlette's `TestClient`, backed by a real per-test SQLite database (not mocks), so persistence and auth paths run for real.
- **Modules exercised (through the seam only)**: auth (register/login/refresh/logout), users (list/me/role/delete), tasks (list/get/create/update/delete/bulk), password.
- **Prior art**: none yet (greenfield) — this spec establishes the pattern; later specs should follow it.
- **Coverage emphasis**: authorization boundaries (member vs admin, own-vs-other task), the status machine (including `done`-on-create rejection and unblock return-to-prior), refresh rotation + reuse detection, last-admin guard, and the RFC 9457 error shape + stable `code` set.

## Out of Scope

The following are deferred (tracked as separate GitHub issues, not part of this spec):

- Settings module (user preferences, theme, language).
- Password reset / forgot-password.
- Profile management beyond `GET /users/me` (e.g. updating one's own name/email).
- Account status / soft-disable ("suspended").
- Search suggestions/autocomplete beyond the `q` substring filter.
- Third-party integrations (payment, shipping, marketing).
- Bulk delete for tasks.
- General rate limiting beyond the auth endpoints.

## Further Notes

- The contract already lives in `docs/openapi.yaml`; the implementation's generated OpenAPI should be diffed against it in CI to catch drift (the "OpenAPI schema diff" requirement).
- The domain vocabulary is defined in `GLOSSARY.md`; use those terms (e.g. "assignee", not "owner"/"handler") in code, tests, and issue titles.
- Three ADRs apply: single-tenant workspace, stateful refresh-token sessions, and fixed two-role authorization — the implementation must not quietly deviate from them.
title: Implement Template Dashboard API

body:
### Problem & Solution Overview

The original Bose app had a sleep timer. OCT cannot stop a speaker after a while, so users fall asleep with the radio running all night.

**Solution:** a server-side **sleep timer per device**: after N minutes the volume is faded out, playback is stopped (or the device is put into standby) and the previous volume is restored, so the next playback is not silent. It uses only calls OCT already makes (`press_key`, `get_volume`, `set_volume`, `get_now_playing`). This issue also introduces the shared **`VolumeFader`**, the shared **`stop_playback`** helper and a **stateful mock device**, which the follow-up issue "Scheduled actions (alarms)" reuses.

### User stories
- As a listener I want to start a 30-minute sleep timer from the device control page so the speaker turns itself off while I fall asleep.
- As a listener I want to see the remaining time and cancel the timer.

### Decisions (already made — do not re-open)
- **One active timer per device**; starting a new one replaces the old one. Timers are per device only (no zone propagation). All start/replace/cancel/fire operations of one device are serialised by a per-device `asyncio.Lock`.
- All device access goes through `DeviceService` (`get_now_playing`, `get_volume`, `set_volume`, `press_key(device_id, key, state)` with the string keys `PAUSE`, `STOP`, `POWER`) — **always live calls, never the state cache**. Do not use `DeviceService.send_key` (it validates against `KeyType` and returns a fresh now-playing). The service receives its `DeviceService` from the lifespan.
- Helpers in `devices/playback.py` (unit-tested): `is_standby(info) = info.source == "STANDBY"`; `is_playing(info) = info.state in {"PLAY_STATE","BUFFERING_STATE"}`; `async stop_playback(device_service, device_id, sleep)`: if playing → `press_key("PAUSE")`, wait 2 s, re-read now-playing, and if still `PLAY_STATE` → `press_key("STOP")`. "Device unreachable" = `DeviceConnectionError`; retries apply only to it (an invalid key name must not trigger retries).
- The timer outcome is **logged only**; no outcome is stored or exposed. The UI therefore says "Timer is no longer active", never "ended".
- Behaviour of PAUSE/STOP/POWER on real devices (PAUSE on streams, STOP on other sources, `set_volume` while paused, POWER right after STOP — a 1 s delay is inserted before `POWER`) is an **assumption verified by the maintainers on hardware**, not by this issue. Reported latency of remote commands (#261 "Time lag zwischen Remote-Action und Ausführung", up to ~15 s) is handled by absolute step deadlines (below).
- The timer waits using the **wall clock** in chunks of ≤ 30 s (re-checking `now >= target`), with `clock`/`sleep` injected into the service constructor — no single long `sleep()`.
- Table `sleep_timers` is created in `_create_schema()`; the version range **425–449** is reserved for later `_apply_migration` changes. No foreign key to `devices`.

---

## Part A — Backend

### A.1 Modules
`apps/backend/src/opencloudtouch/sleep_timer/`: `__init__.py`, `models.py`, `repository.py`, `service.py` (`SleepTimerService`; public `start(...)`, `cancel(device_id, *, restore_volume=True)`; created in `_init_services` **before any mock-mode early return**, `app.state.sleep_timer_service`, stopped in `_shutdown` before repositories close), `api/routes.py` (own router registered in `main.py`; `get_sleep_timer_service` in `core/dependencies.py`). Shared: `devices/volume_fader.py`, `devices/playback.py`.
Table: `device_id` PK, `ends_at` (UTC), `duration_minutes`, `fade_seconds`, `end_action` (`stop`|`standby`), `original_volume` (nullable), `created_at`.

### A.2 `VolumeFader`
`class FadeResult(StrEnum): COMPLETED, MANUAL_CHANGE, DEVICE_ERROR`. `VolumeFader(device_service, sleep, clock)` with `async fade(device_id, from_v, to_v, seconds, *, skip_if_muted=True) -> FadeResult`:
1. `seconds == 0`, `from_v == to_v`, or (`skip_if_muted` and the device is muted) → no fade, `COMPLETED`.
2. `steps = min(150, max(1, ceil(seconds / 2)))`; step `i` (1..steps) targets `int(from_v + (to_v - from_v) * i / steps + 0.5)` (the last step is exactly `to_v`); a `set_volume` is skipped when the value equals the previous one. Step `i` is due at `start + i * seconds/steps` (**absolute deadlines**: a slow device does not stretch the fade; if the clock is already past the end, jump to the last step).
3. `last_set_by_us` starts at `from_v`. Before each step read `get_volume().target`; if `abs(read - last_set_by_us) > 2` → `MANUAL_CHANGE` (the user's volume is left alone).
4. A `DeviceConnectionError` is retried per step (3 × 20 s); if still failing → `DEVICE_ERROR`.
The schedules issue uses the same class with `skip_if_muted=False` for fade-in.

### A.3 Timer behaviour
1. `PUT` validates the device exists and answers a live `get_volume` (503 otherwise), persists the row and arms the task. **Replacing** an existing timer first cancels it and, if its `original_volume` is set and the volume is still within ±2 of the last value we set (or ≤ 2), restores it before arming the new one (the new timer's V0 is the pre-fade volume).
2. At `fade_start = ends_at - fade_seconds` (= `ends_at` if `fade_seconds == 0`): read `V0 = get_volume().actual`. If `fade_seconds > 0` and V0 > 0 and not muted: **persist `original_volume = V0` first**, then run the fade `V0 → 0`. Otherwise no fade, `original_volume` stays null and no restore happens.
3. End sequence, in this order: `stop_playback`; then **restore the volume** to `original_volume` (best effort, failure logged) if one is stored and `get_volume().target <= 2`; then, if `end_action == "standby"` and the device is not in standby: wait 1 s and `press_key("POWER")`. If the device was not playing, the stop part is skipped. The row is deleted at the end.
4. `MANUAL_CHANGE` during the fade → the timer ends without stop/standby (logged `manual_change`) and the row is deleted.
5. **Failure handling:** a `DeviceConnectionError` during the fade (`DEVICE_ERROR`) or the end sequence is retried (3 retries, 20 s apart — 4 attempts total); if it still fails, log ERROR, delete the row, leave the volume as is. `DeviceNotFoundError` at fire time → delete the row, log.
6. **Startup recovery:** a row with `ends_at` in the past by **≤ 10 min** runs the end sequence (the user is presumably still asleep); older → only restore `original_volume` if set (same ≤ 2 rule). The row is kept until the restore succeeds (retried in the background with the 3 × 20 s policy). Rows in the future are re-armed; if such a row has `original_volume` set, restore it first and start the fade over with `min(fade_seconds, remaining)`; if `remaining < 2 s` skip the fade.
7. **Shutdown:** in-flight fades are cancelled and `original_volume` is restored best-effort within a single `asyncio.wait_for(..., 3)` around all timers in parallel.
8. `cancel(device_id, restore_volume=True)` is the code path of `DELETE` and is called by the schedules issue.

### A.4 REST API (`/api/devices/{device_id}/sleep-timer`; contract shared with Part B)
One response model `SleepTimerStatus`: `active: bool`, `server_time` (both required), and `device_id`, `ends_at`, `duration_minutes`, `fade_seconds`, `end_action`, `state: "running"|"fading"|"ending"` (null when inactive). `state` is computed from the clock: `fading` iff `server_time >= ends_at - fade_seconds` and before `ends_at`; `ending` iff `server_time >= ends_at` while the row still exists (end sequence running).
- `PUT` body `{duration_minutes: 1..720, fade_seconds: 0..300 = 30, end_action: "stop"|"standby" = "stop"}` → `200` `SleepTimerStatus(active=true)`. `duration_minutes` is required. `fade_seconds > duration_minutes*60` → `422` code `sleep_timer_fade_too_long`, path `fade_seconds` (raised with `raise_coded(422, …, field="fade_seconds")` from the route). Pydantic range errors give `validation_error`. Unknown device → `404 device_not_found`; unreachable → `503 device_unreachable`.
- `GET` → always `200 SleepTimerStatus` (`active:false` when none); makes **no device call**; `404 device_not_found` for unknown devices.
- `DELETE` → `204`, idempotent, never 503 (restore failures are logged); a running fade is cancelled and `cancel()` restores `original_volume` under the ±2 rule. If the end sequence has begun, `DELETE` waits for the per-device lock and returns `204` without interrupting it.

### A.5 Stateful mock device
`MockDeviceClient` (`devices/mock_client.py`) builds a new client per call and keeps `_volume` per instance, `now_playing` comes from shared `MOCK_DEVICES`. Add a **module-level state registry** `dict[device_id, _MockState]` (volume 45, muted, source, play state, standby), initialised lazily from today's defaults/`MOCK_DEVICES`, shared by all instances, copied (never the shared `NowPlayingInfo` object). `set_volume` clamps to 0–100 and sets actual and target; `PLAY`→`PLAY_STATE`; `PAUSE`→`PAUSE_STATE` (only if playing); `STOP`→`STOP_STATE`; `POWER` toggles standby (source `STANDBY`/`STOP_STATE` ↔ `INTERNET_RADIO`/`PLAY_STATE`); `PRESET_n`→`INTERNET_RADIO`/`PLAY_STATE` and wakes from standby. Add `STOP` to the key whitelist. Provide `reset_mock_state()` and an autouse test fixture (`tests/conftest.py`) calling it; existing tests asserting the defaults still pass. Unit tests for the service may use a fake `DeviceService`.

### A.6 Acceptance criteria — Backend
1. **Given** `PUT {duration_minutes: 30, fade_seconds: 30}` on a mock device playing at volume 40, **when** the injected clock advances 30 min, **then** volume calls follow the fader formula for 15 steps ending at 0 (assert the formula and the final 0, not hand-typed numbers), `PAUSE` is pressed, the volume is restored to 40, and `GET` returns `active:false`.
2. **Given** `end_action:"standby"`, **then** the order is PAUSE → restore volume → `POWER`; a device already in standby gets no `POWER`.
3. **Given** `DELETE` mid-fade, **then** the fade stops and the volume returns to V0 (only if still ≤ 2 / within ±2); a second `DELETE` returns 204; `DELETE` during the end sequence waits and returns 204.
4. **Given** the user changes the volume during the fade (the test sleep callback mutates the mock registry), **then** the fade aborts, nothing is paused, the user's volume stays and the row is deleted.
5. **Given** a second `PUT` during a fade, **then** V0 is restored first and the new timer's V0 equals the pre-fade volume (never the faded value).
6. **Given** `fade_seconds=0`, **then** no volume change happens before `PAUSE` and no restore; **given** V0 = 0 or muted, no fade and no restore.
7. **Given** `fade_seconds > duration*60`, **then** 422 `sleep_timer_fade_too_long` with `errors[].path = "fade_seconds"`; out-of-range values → `validation_error`; unknown device → 404 `device_not_found`; unreachable → 503 `device_unreachable`.
8. **Given** the mock raises `DeviceConnectionError` on the 7th `set_volume`, **then** the step is retried 3 × 20 s (fake clock); after exhaustion the row is deleted and an ERROR is logged.
9. **Given** a restart with a timer ending in 10 min, **then** a fresh service on the same DB fires on time; **given** a timer elapsed 5 min ago, the end sequence runs; **given** one elapsed 30 min ago with `original_volume`, only the volume is restored (row kept until it succeeds).
10. **Given** the device is not playing at the end, **then** no `PAUSE` is sent; **given** `PAUSE` leaves `PLAY_STATE`, `STOP` is sent.
11. **Given** `GET` without a timer, **then** `200 {active:false, server_time}`; during the end sequence `state:"ending"`; during the fade `state:"fading"`.
12. `VolumeFader` tests cover the step formula, step cap 150, absolute deadlines, abort on manual change, equal volumes, `seconds=0`, duplicate-value skipping and `skip_if_muted=False`; `is_standby`/`is_playing`/`stop_playback` are unit-tested.
13. Works in `OCT_MOCK_MODE=true`: start → fade → pause is observable via `DeviceService.get_volume`/`get_now_playing`; existing mock-client tests still pass.
14. `openapi.yaml` updated; `docs/CONFIGURATION.md` section **"Sleep timer"** (behaviour, fade, end actions, restart behaviour, hardware assumptions).

---

## Part B — Frontend

Placement: **Local Control page** (`pages/LocalControl.tsx`, route `/local`), per selected device, near the volume controls. New component `components/SleepTimer.tsx`, hook `hooks/useSleepTimer.ts`, client `api/sleepTimer.ts`. Visual design by the designer.

### B.1 Functional requirements
1. **Start:** duration from presets (15/30/45/60/90/120 min, default 30) or a custom integer 1–720 (empty/non-numeric/out of range → inline error); fade selectable (off = `0`, 10 s, 30 s, 60 s; default 30 s) — options longer than the duration are disabled; end action (stop / standby). Last-used values are stored in `localStorage` under `oct.sleepTimer.defaults` as `{duration, fade, endAction}` (wrapped in try/catch; restored values are validated and a fade larger than the duration is clamped).
2. **Active timer** (`active:true`): a live countdown, the end action and a **cancel** action. The countdown is computed from `ends_at` and a **server clock offset** (`server_time` vs `Date.now()` at receipt), format `m:ss` below 1 h and `h:mm:ss` otherwise. The "fading" and "ending" indications are derived locally from `ends_at`, `fade_seconds` and the offset; `state` is only used for the first render.
3. When the countdown reaches 0 show "ending…" and refetch every 3 s (max 90 s) until `active:false`; then show the neutral message "Timer is no longer active" once. If a poll returns `active:false` **before** `ends_at` (cancelled elsewhere, manual volume change), return to the "start" state without a message.
4. Refetch when the device changes, when the tab becomes visible and after start/cancel; otherwise poll at most every 30 s while visible and not in "ending".
5. Starting while a timer exists replaces it silently (the UI shows the new end time).
6. For an offline device (reuse the page's `deviceOffline` value) the start control is disabled with an explanation; a running timer stays displayed and cancel still works. Errors map through `ApiError.code`: `sleep_timer_fade_too_long` at the fade control, `device_unreachable`, `device_not_found`, generic.

### B.2 Accessibility
The countdown has an accessible name and is **not** announced every second (announce start, cancel and "no longer active" via a polite live region); duration/fade controls are labelled; cancel is keyboard operable.

### B.3 Acceptance criteria — Frontend
1. **Given** a 30-min timer with fade 30 s and stop, **then** `PUT` carries exactly those values and the countdown matches `ends_at` against the server clock (±1 s) — also with `Date` mocked 5 minutes off.
2. **Given** an active timer, **when** cancelled, **then** `DELETE` is sent and the control returns to "start".
3. **Given** a 1-minute duration, **then** fade options above 60 s are disabled; a custom value `0` or `721` shows the inline error and sends nothing.
4. **Given** an offline device, **then** start is disabled with the explanation and cancel still works.
5. **Given** `GET` returns `active:false`, **then** no error toast; **given** the countdown hit 0 and polls return `active:true` then `active:false`, "ending…" then the neutral message are shown once; **given** `active:false` before `ends_at`, no message.
6. **Given** a page reload with an active timer, **then** the countdown continues from the server data; polling stops while the tab is hidden.
7. **Given** `sleep_timer_fade_too_long`, **then** the translated error is shown at the fade control.
8. Remembered defaults are restored (and clamped); the page works when storage throws.
9. All strings (incl. `errors.api.sleep_timer_fade_too_long`) in 10 locales; Vitest tests for countdown/offset logic, option disabling and flows; Cypress `apps/frontend/tests/e2e/sleep-timer.cy.ts` with `cy.intercept`.

---

## Out of scope
Scheduled alarms (separate issue), per-zone timers, push notification when the timer finishes, snooze, storing the outcome, hardware verification of standby/POWER semantics (maintainers verify on real devices and file bugs).

## Related issues
- Depends on #535 ("Machine-readable `code` in API error responses").
- Follow-up: "Scheduled actions (alarms)" uses `VolumeFader`, `stop_playback`, `SleepTimerService.cancel` and the stateful mock.
- #261 "Time lag zwischen Remote-Action und Ausführung" — command latency; hence absolute step deadlines.
- PRs "feat(frontend): add device bass settings UI" and "fix(ui): responsive layout, accessibility and wizard redesign" also edit the Local Control page; hence the separate component.

---

## Cross-cutting requirements (apply to Part A and Part B)

- **Prerequisites:** if this issue names a prerequisite issue (marked "Depends on"), **do not start until that issue's PRs are merged** — check on `main` that its files exist. If they are not there, stop and comment on this issue; never re-implement a prerequisite inside this PR (parallel runs would create conflicting copies).
- **Delivery order:** unless the "Decisions" section of this issue defines another split, Part A (backend) and Part B (frontend) are delivered as **two PRs**, A first (it updates `apps/backend/openapi.yaml`), then B (runs `npm run generate:api` in `apps/frontend` and commits `api/generated/schema.ts`). Where the frontend uses hand-written API types (`api/presets.ts`, `api/restore.ts`), B updates them by hand to match the OpenAPI schema. Each PR must pass all gates on its own. Open PRs that edit the same files (responsive-layout/wizard redesign, bass-settings UI, restore-wizard styling, backup-verification) will conflict: rebase on `main` after they merge and keep their markup; never resolve a conflict by reverting someone else's change.
- **Error contract:** failures of new endpoints use the standard `ErrorDetail` body **with the `code` field** from "Machine-readable `code` in API error responses" (#535; `core/exceptions.py`, `core/error_codes.py`). Validation failures list `errors[]` entries `{field, path, message, code}`; **`path`** is the field path relative to the body (`port`, `config.url`) and is what this issue's frontend uses (`field` keeps its legacy form such as `body.port`). Domain codes are raised with `raise_coded(status, code, detail, field=…)` or, for field validators, `ValueError("code:<name>")`. Status convention for new endpoints: 404 not found, 409 conflict/state, 413 too large, 422 validation, 502 upstream service failed, 503 device unreachable (`device_unreachable`), 504 upstream timeout. Never put secrets, stack traces, filesystem paths or raw exception text into `detail`, `params` or `extra`.
- **Backend conventions:** Python 3.11+, async, type hints. Domain modules follow `[domain]/{__init__,service,repository}.py` + `api/routes.py` registered in `main.py` (`adapter.py` only when talking to an external system; routes of an existing domain may stay in its router). SQLite via `BaseRepository`: create tables with `CREATE TABLE/INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` in `_create_schema()` (the repositories' pattern); `_apply_migration(version, description, sql)` executes **one** statement and is only for later schema changes in the version range reserved by this issue (versions are global across repositories — grep `_apply_migration(` first). Where `ON DELETE CASCADE` is used, the repository executes `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON` right after connecting (it is per connection and `BaseRepository` does not set it; do not change `BaseRepository`) and a test proves the cascade. Register repositories in `repo_classes` in `main.py`, create services in `_init_services` (before any mock-mode early return when the feature must also work in mock mode), stop them in `_shutdown` before repositories close. XML only via `defusedxml`. Datetimes are UTC ISO-8601 with `Z`. New config fields go into `AppConfig` (`core/config.py`, env prefix `OCT_`).
- **Frontend conventions:** React 19, TypeScript strict, functional components, TanStack Query for server state where the surrounding code uses it (note: some existing hooks such as `usePresets` and the Diagnostics page use plain state), `useMutation` for POST actions, hooks in `hooks/`, API clients in `api/`, new pages registered in `App.tsx` before the catch-all (pages sit inside the "devices required" guard), navigation links in `components/Navigation.tsx` via its `withDevice` helper when the issue says so, shared UI from `components/` (`Modal`, `ConfirmDialog`, `Toast`, `EmptyState`, `LoadingSkeleton`). Translate backend failures with `getApiErrorMessage` / `getFieldErrors` ((#535), keys `errors.api.<code>`); unknown codes fall back to a generic message containing the raw code.
- **Design handoff:** the visual design is delivered separately by a designer. Part B specifies **behaviour, data, states and accessibility only**. Implement with existing design-system components so the UI is usable and consistent. If designer mockups are attached to this issue (or linked in a comment) when it is picked up, align the markup with them without changing the behaviour defined here. Do not block on mockups.
- **i18n:** every new user-facing string gets a key in **all 10 locales** (`apps/frontend/src/i18n/locales/`: de, en, es, fr, it, ja, nl, pl, pt-BR, sv). English and German are written properly; the others may be machine-quality but never empty and never left in English, with identical `{{placeholders}}`. The open PR "test(i18n): check interpolation placeholders across locales" adds a parity test — do not depend on it; add key-presence and placeholder checks for your keys to your own tests if it is not merged.
- **Tests / gates:** backend `cd apps/backend && python -m pytest tests/unit/ -x -q`, `ruff check src/`, `mypy src/opencloudtouch/`; frontend `npx vitest run`, `npx eslint src/`, `npx tsc --noEmit`; coverage ≥ 80 %; Bandit-clean. Cypress specs live in `apps/frontend/tests/e2e/*.cy.ts` and use `cy.intercept` (see `tests/e2e/support/`). Time-dependent backend tests use injectable clock/sleep (no real waiting). Reference code by names, not line numbers.
- **Docs:** user-visible behaviour and every new env var go into `docs/CONFIGURATION.md` under the heading named in this issue (GitHub anchors must resolve); add a `CHANGELOG.md` entry under *Unreleased*; update the README feature list when the feature is user-visible.
- **Security model:** OCT is a trusted-LAN service (`.github/SECURITY.md`); this issue adds no authentication. Log `scheme://host:port` only, never full URLs that may carry tokens.
title: [Spec]: Sleep timer — fade out and stop a SoundTouch device after a countdown

body:
## Goal Continuously verify that connectors in `@kbn/connector-specs`: 1. **Work**: every connector checked into the repo, with all its actions, works when invoked from Agent Builder (as tools) and from Workflows (as steps). 2. **Haven't drifted**: the vendor API surface each connector depends on has not changed since the connector was written or last updated. When either check fails, the owning engineers find out, and an updated connector can be produced largely automatically and lands through a normal reviewed PR. ## Constraints - We don't want to keep (paid) vendor credentials for long stretches of time. We want to use trial accounts as much as possible, and when these trials lapse verification and drift protection should remain functional. - Vendors have different API contract types. Of the current ~85 connectors in Kibana we have OpenAPI (Swagger 2, 3.0, 3.1), Google Discovery, AWS Smithy, GraphQL, MCP-backed, and vendors with no machine-readable specs. All formats with a spec should be supported. A connector without a usable spec is exempt, with the reason recorded. - Connector types are compiled into Kibana and only registerable during the actions plugin's setup phase; a running Kibana cannot load a newly edited spec. ## Approach - **Introduce Connector emulator package** (`@kbn/connector-emulate`). This package allows serving of API mocks based on vendor specs. It should offer an in-house OpenAPI adapter (Swagger 2, 3.0, 3.1, 3.2) using Kibana's existing `@cfworker/json-schema`, plus GraphQL and MCP adapters. - The emulator package handles requests, serves responses, emulates each vendor's pagination style, enforces advertised bounds, and applies overlays. - The emulator package allows two modes of operation: in-process as a standard `fetch` first (milestone 1), and later as an HTTP forward proxy that a running Kibana talks to (milestone 2). - The emulator package should allow **recordings** of real vendor traffic captured at creation time of the Connector (with trial credentials). The recordings should be sanitized and committed inside the repo, so realistic mock data outlives the trial account. - **Weekly drift detection** classifying changes as breaking / non-breaking / deprecation and recording each connector against a snapshot mock and a latest-spec mock. The two together decide the outcome: healthy connectors with only non-breaking changes get a bot PR, and anything else that needs attention gets a deduplicated per-connector issue mentioning the CODEOWNERS teams. - **Connector updates**: Non-breaking spec changes are refreshed automatically by the pipeline's bot PR. Breaking changes are fixed with the `update-connector` skill where a developer is, and land through a normal reviewed PR. Running the skill headlessly with the `ai:update-connector` label (#300064) is optional, if drift issues pile up. - **Storing vendor contract artifacts** per connector (`vendor_api/`): spec source, an action → vendor operation map recorded by running each handler against a mock (not hand-written), and a trimmed, normalized snapshot per vendor spec source of only the operations used. Per-operation pagination descriptors; vendor spec corrections as an OpenAPI Overlay (`overlay.yaml`). - **AWS Smithy** models are converted to OpenAPI by the emulator (`restJson1`, `restXml`) and loaded by the recorder, so those connectors can be recorded (#299512). `awsJson` services (CloudWatch) are described as marked OpenAPI documents with one `POST /` per operation, served by `X-Amz-Target` (#302325, implemented in #302326). - **Static contract test** at PR time: recorded map matches the committed map; zod inputs are compatible with vendor parameters and at least as strict as vendor bounds; vendor API coverage never shrinks (a recorded connector keeps its artifacts, and a new one has artifacts or an exemption). ## Inbound events Connectors can also receive vendor webhooks: a spec's `events` declares event definitions and a `handleEvents` that turns a vendor body into typed events. #303869 has `create-connector` add them whenever the vendor pushes webhooks. Six connectors have them today: `.datadog`, `.github`, `.microsoft-teams`, `.servicenow_search`, `.slack2` (with actions) and `.inboundWebhook` (events only). **Not covered yet.** Spec capture, the contract test and drift detection check only what a connector sends: the recorder runs `actions` and never calls `handleEvents`. The events tests check `handleEvents` against the connector's own event schemas, written from vendor docs, not against what the vendor sends. **Why it matters.** When a vendor renames or moves a webhook field, or the docs were wrong from the start, `handleEvents` no longer recognizes the body and emits no events, which is also its answer for a body it deliberately ignores. Nothing fails: workflows stop starting, and no case or alert is created. Outbound breakage shows up as a failed call; this doesn't. **Where vendors describe webhooks** (checked 2026-11-06 unless noted): - **GitHub**: its pinned REST description has `x-webhooks` (275 entries, each with a body schema). - **Microsoft Teams** (checked 2026-11-10): partly. The pinned Graph description has no webhook entries, but defines `changeNotificationCollection` under `components/schemas`. It types the envelope (`changeType`, `lifecycleEvent`, `tenantId`), not what `handleEvents` parses: the `resource` path that supplies every ID, and `resourceData` beyond `@odata.type`. - **Slack**: an Events API AsyncAPI document last changed in 2018. - **Datadog** and **ServiceNow**: the body is a user-written template or configured per instance, so there's no vendor contract. **Decision** (2026-11-10): checking `handleEvents` against vendor webhook schemas waits. A vendor spec would check one connector fully and one partly, against the cost of an `events` manifest map, webhook projection, a contract test on sampled bodies, `--drift` wiring and `oasdiff` support for `webhooks`. The silent failure is caught for every connector, schema or not, by a runtime signal and by real recorded bodies. In order: 1. The connector skills say that `vendor_api/` covers a connector's actions only, once #303869 lets them add `events`. 2. Runtime signal: count ingest requests that emitted no events, per connector type (#302334). The inbound request counter can't tell these apart today: it reports `accepted` either way, without the connector type. 3. Emulating inbound events (#304376): event fixtures, sending events from the emulator to Kibana's ingest URL, vendor handshakes, and follow-up lookups that match the event. It doesn't depend on vendor schemas; Kibana authenticates ingest with its own token, and no connector verifies a vendor signature. 4. Recorded webhooks: the live verification pass (#295691) captures real, sanitized bodies at the ingest route as event fixtures. 5. Later, once enough connectors with events come from vendors that publish webhook schemas: a manifest `events` map (a webhook, or a named body schema such as Teams'), snapshots that keep those schemas, and `handleEvents` in the contract test and `--drift`. Coverage reporting (#303327) then counts events separately from actions. ## Research - We explored using Prism. The Prism spike worked, but Prism was dropped. See #295684. - We have looked at Vercel's emulate. Our approach was 80% created by ourselves before we were made aware of Emulate, but we borrowed some ideas with regards to an OAuth authorization endpoint, spec-driven scope checks, and an async Responder seam for stateful responses (API ideas from [vercel-labs/emulate](https://github.com/vercel-labs/emulate); see https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/298854–https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/298858). ## Milestones The Connector Emulator package is delivered in two milestones. **Milestone 1: the package allows an in-process mock (no server).** A `fetch` by connector code is answered in memory, by plugging into the connector's axios client in Jest. - Brings: the recorder (action → operation map, projected snapshot), the static contract test, recording against the pinned and the latest-spec mock for functional drift detection, Tier A's response-side checks, and the fast loop of the `update-connector` skill (contract test + Tier A, run locally or optionally in `gh-aw`). - Runs on standard runners with no Kibana, ES, ports, network or credentials. - Covers the **drift** goal fully, and the **works** goal for each connector's own code: the requests its handlers send and how they handle every response the spec allows. - Doesn't see what sits between a user and the handler: the actions plugin's pipeline (connector creation, encrypted secrets, its own auth and HTTP client setup, proxy/TLS settings, payload limits, error mapping), Workflows steps, Agent Builder tool calls, and SDK/MCP clients leased through `ctx.getClient`. **Milestone 2: server mode.** The same core behind an HTTP forward proxy; Kibana is started with `xpack.actions.proxyUrl` pointing at it, and trusts a throwaway CA so the mock can terminate TLS for vendor hosts. - Brings: Tier B (actions API + Workflows), Tier C (Agent Builder evals), a pass-through recording fallback for traffic that bypasses `ctx.client`, and deterministic, credential-free Scout/FTR runs and local development for features built on connectors (a spec-driven alternative to the hand-written `actions_simulators`). - Completes the **works** goal for Agent Builder and Workflows. - Depends on running Kibana + ES in CI and, for Tier C, an LLM plus recordings or fixtures, since sampled data has the right shape but no meaning. ## Overview diagram ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph create ["1. full vendor spec"] recorder["Run every action handler

If so, how exactly (as a Buildkite pipeline? Ensemble? Github Action?) **Decided:** scheduled checks run as a Buildkite pipeline (#295692); Tier B joins it as further steps (#295694). - **Exemption categories.** Reasons in `vendor_api_exemptions.json` are free text, so "no HTTP API" (permanent) can't be told from "needs credentials to fetch a spec" (temporary). Tag each entry with a category, which changes the file's schema across open PRs, so it should land first on `main`. To be done in #303327. - **Credentials for spec fetches.** 9 connectors need credentials to fetch their spec (`.box`, `.buildkite`, `.dropbox`, `.tavily_mcp`, `.new_relic`, `.dynatrace`, `.servicenow_search`, `.salesforce`, `.workday`). Captured once, they get the contract test and the emulator, but no automatic drift detection. Is that enough, or is a narrow exception to "no long-lived vendor credentials" worth it for fetching specs? - **Spec sources.** Where a vendor doesn't publish a spec at a stable URL, do we pin a community-maintained spec, or treat the connector as exempt? The survey found 6 such connectors. - **Inbound events.** Only GitHub publishes a current webhook schema among today's connectors with events. Which phase does the inbound work belong to, and should the runtime signal or the schema checks come first? **Decided:** the runtime signal and emulation first; schema checks wait (see "Inbound events"). - **LLM for Tier C.** The OpenRouter secret the existing `gh-aw` workflows use, or an Elastic inference endpoint? - **Ownership.** The drift pipeline is owned by `workflows-eng` (#300055). Parent: #1 | Lane: UI (owns `ui/**` only) | Priority: P1 | Estimate: 5 pts | Depends on: STAR-2 (#3)

## Context
The UI is the MVP and must look finished. It is built against `docs/api/openapi.yaml` and a local mock so it does not wait for the API lane.

## Changes
- [ ] Create `ui/` with the current stable Angular CLI: standalone components, signals, strict TypeScript, SCSS, the CLI's default test runner, ESLint.
- [ ] Angular Material as the component base with a custom dark "mission control" theme (CSS variables for colors, spacing and typography); app shell with toolbar, navigation, responsive layout, 404 page.
- [ ] Typed API client generated from `docs/api/openapi.yaml` with a public generator (script in `package.json`, generated code not hand-edited); a thin service layer on top using `HttpClient`; base URL from environment config.
- [ ] Stateful mock API in `ui/mock-server` (Node, runs on port 3000, loads seed people/duties from the contract examples) supporting all six routes including add person, rename, and add duty, with the same status codes and error envelope, and it enforces the contract's required-reason rule (reason required when the start date is after today UTC, before the person's latest duty start, or when the latest duty is `RETIRED`; otherwise 400 with a field error on `reason`) so the UI reason flow can be exercised. `npm run start:mock` starts it; `npm start` runs the app against it.
- [ ] A global HTTP interceptor that maps the error envelope to a typed `ApiError`.
- [ ] "Acting as" control in the toolbar: asks for a name once (stored in localStorage, editable, 1 to 100 chars) and an interceptor sends it as the `X-Actor` header on every write request. Write actions stay disabled with a hint until a name is set. Label it as self-declared. The mock rejects writes without `X-Actor` with the contract 400.
- [ ] README section in `ui/README.md` with install/run/test commands.

## Acceptance criteria
- `npm ci`, `npm run lint`, `npm test`, `npm run build` all pass on a fresh clone.
- The app starts against the mock and shows the shell with no console errors.
- Changing `openapi.yaml` and re-running the generator updates the client; the build fails if the app uses a removed type.
- The mock returns the contract's 404/409/400 examples for the documented triggers (unknown name, duplicate name, invalid input).
- A test proves writes carry `X-Actor` and are blocked in the UI until a name is set.
- Run-and-look: screenshot of the shell at desktop and phone widths in the PR.
title: STAR-10 [UI] Scaffold Angular app, shell, theme, generated API client, mock API

body:
# Why this issue?

As we're close to release Microcks `1.16` , we realized that most of the items on the roadmap are more of shallow evolutions (new protocols to support, new formats to support,...) and technical upgrades than real new big features... The last 2 years have been focused on making the project more stable, robust, open to the community - maybe to the detriment of bringing big new stuff.

Microcks 1.x has grown organically for years and is used in more and more demanding contexts (large enterprises, CI/CD at scale, and now AI agents and MCP servers). Before committing to a roadmap, I would like to open the discussion with the community on what a **Microcks 2.0** could be.

What follows is the state of an early study. **Nothing is decided unless explicitly stated**: these are ideas, trade-offs and open questions, grouped by theme. Please challenge them, add your own, and tell us what matters most to you.

A few guiding principles for the discussion:

- The **API contract remains the source of truth** for mocks and tests.
- **Backward compatibility** matters: in particular, the API consumed by the Microcks CLI must remain *ideally* compatible - if not it should be close with paved guidelines on how to adapt.
- New capabilities are **opt-in**; the default behavior (stateless, deterministic mocks) is preserved.
- The **Uber distribution** (single process, embedded database) must stay simple and lightweight.
- No performance or compatibility claim without evidence.

Legend: ✅ decided (for the study) · 🔎 to explore · 💡 idea

# What's in it?

## 1. Technical foundation

### Database: keep MongoDB, on a recent version 🔎
- MongoDB 4.4 (used in our compose files) is end-of-life; 5.0 and 6.0 as well.
- Pros of MongoDB: no rigid schema or migrations, embeddable in memory for the Uber distribution, good performance, many managed offerings.
- Cons we checked: version upgrade needed, lower enterprise adoption than PostgreSQL in some surveys, **SSPL license (not OSI-approved)**. We did not demonstrate any size/performance issue with recent versions yet.
- Alternatives considered: FerretDB (MongoDB wire-compatible, Apache 2.0), or PostgreSQL with JSONB (large rewrite and migration effort). **Not retained for 2.0**, but we may revisit later.
- Open points:
  - 🔎 Target version, and the **AVX CPU requirement** of MongoDB 5.0+.
  - 🔎 How the Uber distribution gets an embedded database compatible with the target version.
  - 🔎 **CNCF position on the SSPL**: to be confirmed with the CNCF, as this is not settled by our decision.
  - 🔎 Upgrade notes for 4.4 users (step-by-step major upgrades).
  - 🔎 Consider DocumentDB (MongoDB wire-compatible, MIT) as an alternative during development to avoid licensing or distribution issues

### Replace Spring Boot with Quarkus (webapp) 🔎
- Motivations: Spring Boot feels heavy, OpenTelemetry was painful to set up during the Spring Boot 4 migration, the async minion already runs on Quarkus, and it opens the door to faster startup, lower memory, native builds and a single stack.
- The coupling to Spring is strong but concentrated in three areas: servlet-based mock processing, Mongo persistence, and security. The rest is mostly mechanical.
- A **parallel rewrite** (without touching the 1.x code) has been started as a feasibility study: Quarkus with Panache MongoDB, CDI events, JAX-RS controllers (REST, SOAP, GraphQL, gRPC, MCP and the `/api` endpoints), SmallRye Kafka. The port builds and its test suite passes. Security is intentionally left out for now.
- Open points: behavior compatibility of mocks and APIs, contributor familiarity, native-mode validation, measured (not assumed) startup and memory gains.

### Modular code base 🔎
- The `io.github.microcks.util` package should been split into **Maven modules per artifact format** (OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, GraphQL, gRPC, SoapUI, Postman, HAR, metadata, and the newly added OpenCollection), each holding its importer and its test runner, on top of small shared core modules.
- Hard-coded importer/exporter/test-runner factories are replaced by **`ServiceLoader`-based registries**, a first step toward a real plugin model (see below).
- Migration of Java package: from `io.github.microcks` to `io.microcks`

### Web UI technical base 🔎
- The UI mixes Angular Material with PatternFly 3, Bootstrap 5 and jQuery, and has few tests.
- Direction: a single component base with design tokens, a documented design system, UI journey tests (Playwright) and visual regression **before** the big refactoring, then migration screen by screen rather than a big bang.
- Moving to a new stack has been discarded previously when Patternfly was EOL but it was before the AI-era. We can now start discussing this point again. React? Svelte? 

---

## 2. Multi-tenancy 🔎

- Some adopters already use Microcks to deploy **different mock configurations for the same Service** (for example, artifacts assembled differently).
- Decisions so far:
  - **Tenant and Group are distinct concepts**: a tenant can contain several groups. Group is an authorization-related concept within a tenant
  - A tenant **partitions data**. The same Service can have different mocks in different tenants; its definition is then duplicated per tenant.
- Principle: a deployment without any explicit tenant configuration must see **no extra complexity**, with an implicit `default` tenant, and 100% backward compatibility in single-tenant mode.
- Open questions:
  - What exactly is partitioned (Services, artifacts, tests, secrets, importers)?
  - How does a mock URL identify its tenant (path prefix, header, host) without breaking existing URLs?
  - How is a user associated with several tenants (internal membership with a tenant-level role, tenant selector in the UI, explicit tenant for API/CLI calls)?
  - Isolation approach: partition field vs separate databases. Ideally both should be possible to provide more flexibility on the scale-up model
  - Impact on the async minion (destinations, topics) and on tests.
  - Would a lighter mechanism (named variants of a Service, named artifact sets) be enough for real-life use cases? **Adopters, please tell us how you use this today.**

---

## 3. Authentication and authorization

### Remove the hard dependency on Keycloak 🔎
- By default, Microcks would run **without authentication**, with the ability to plug **any OIDC provider** (Okta, Entra ID, Keycloak, etc.).
- Impacts: backend security layer, web UI token handling (retrieval and refresh, probably Authorization Code + PKCE with the IDP configuration exposed by the backend), async minion, Helm charts and compose files, and the OpenAPI Keycloak configuration endpoint.
- Points of attention: safe defaults (warn when exposed without auth), `user` / `manager` / `admin` roles, compatibility with existing Keycloak deployments.

### Internal Groups and Memberships 🔎
- Replace Keycloak-based group management with a **Group** entity and a **Membership** concept stored in Microcks, managed by Microcks managers and independent from the content of the OIDC token (at least initially; OIDC claims or SCIM could come later).
- The OIDC `sub` identifies a user; the issuer is unique per instance and checked at startup to detect an IDP change.
- Pre-provisioned memberships by email, resolved at first login when the email is verified.
- The model must remain valid when there is no authentication at all.

### Service authentication and migration 💡
- Define the replacement for Keycloak service accounts used by the minions, the CLI and CI pipelines (OIDC client credentials and/or internal API tokens, also useful without an IDP).
- Provide a migration path from an existing Keycloak (users, groups, roles).

---

## 4. Features

### Workflow/End-to-end testing 🔎
The idea is to add a workflow testing perspective based on [Arazzo](https://swagger.io/blog/the-arazzo-specification-a-deep-dive/) and/or allow working on consistent dataset encompassing multiple services mocks. Even without an Arazzo specification, users should be able to review the mocks of a services subset to ensure these examples will allow them to run an end-to-end scenario (ex: subscribe an insurance product, fill a cart and proceed to checkout, etc...). This perspective should allow user to add new synthetic dataset artifacts (aside the existing one) and to package them together to allow versioning and replay.

### Modernized UI and journeys 🔎
- A modern, attractive UI, **including the user journeys**, not only the visual identity.
- Top priority journey: **"first mock in 60 seconds"** (from importing a contract to a usable mock URL in as few steps as possible).
- Keep brand invariants: protocol color spectrum, operational density, light and dark themes.
- Several UX directions have been mocked up for discussion; we will share them once the discussion has started.
- Constraint: the API used by the CLI stays compatible (to be protected with automated contract tests); only the test detail URL used by the CLI needs to remain stable.

### Dashboards 🔎
- **Quality angle**: health of contracts and implementations (success rate per Service/protocol, trends, Services without tests or with stale tests, coverage of operations).
- **"What's new" angle**: recent imports and updates, contract changes between versions, latest test runs.
- Open: which data already exists and which we need to start collecting.

### Scripting and extensibility 🔎
- **JavaScript pre/post-processing scripts**, using the QuickJS4J engine already present, applied to **both mocks and tests** (not to the async part for now). Groovy remains for existing setups.
- **Plugin architecture**: new artifact types (importers), mock controllers and test runners discovered at startup, with the built-in ones consuming the same SPI. Open: in-process vs isolated plugins, plugin manifest and versioning, security of loading third-party code, relationship with the existing minions.

### Microcks as a sandbox platform for AI agents and MCP servers 🔎
The idea is to position Microcks as the way to build **sandboxes representing a whole information system**, usable to evaluate, train and fine-tune agents, agentic workflows and MCP servers. This would be the underlying thread of 2.0. Target audience: first Reshapr users, then existing Microcks adopters moving in that direction. Performance and scalability (many parallel episodes) are an explicit concern.

Building blocks being considered:
- **Stateful mocks and isolated sessions/episodes** (reset, snapshot, fork, seeds, virtual clock), designed together. A promising path is to build on the existing `StateStore` and generic CRUD mocks and to "decorate" the existing dispatching with persistence hooks, instead of scripting dispatch for each state transition.
- 💡**Composed bundles**: multi-service, coherent and versioned datasets.
- 💡 **Fault and adversarial behavior injection**, **trajectory tracing and replay**, **evaluation oracles and scoring** (export for existing evaluation tools: Microcks should provide the simulated world, not become an evaluation framework). See the discussion started by @Apoorva64 on #2371
- **First-class MCP and A2A** (contract, testing, Microcks itself drivable by an agent), building on the existing MCP endpoint.
- 💡 Mocking **LLM APIs** (OpenAI-compatible), assisted generation and learning from traffic, agent-oriented developer experience (SDK, ephemeral mode, light footprint), and an "agent-readiness" score for APIs.

---

## 5. Deployment architecture and eventing 🔎

### Replace Kafka in "full" mode with WebSocket + replica pub/sub 🔎

**Today**
- In the *full* (distributed) deployment, Kafka is used to synchronize the webapp and the async minion: service changes (new, updated, deleted) and async mock triggers are published on dedicated topics (`microcks-services-updates`, `microcks-asyncapi-triggers`).
- In the *Uber* distribution, Kafka is already replaced by a **WebSocket** connection between the webapp and the embedded minion, as there is a single webapp instance.
- Kafka as an infrastructure dependency is often seen as a burden: heavy to deploy, "Microcks-provided Kafka vs. the enterprise Kafka", cost re-invoicing, extra operations, no authentication on the topics today.
- Kafka was introduced to decouple the minions from any specific webapp replica. Note that this is about the **infrastructure** dependency only: Kafka remains a fully supported **mocking and testing protocol** (your own brokers).

**Idea**
- Keep **one single app ↔ minion channel in every deployment mode: WebSocket**. Each minion connects to one webapp replica.
- When running several webapp replicas, relay service-change events **between replicas through an embedded pub/sub** (Hazelcast `ITopic` is the current candidate), so that each replica forwards events to the minions connected to it. This is the same pattern as the one used by [Reshapr](https://github.com/reshaprio/reshapr) between control-plane replicas and gateways.
- The cluster layer sits behind a small interface (event bus). It is **started only when needed** (full mode with several replicas) and **bypassed in Uber mode** (and with a single replica), which stays unchanged.

**Expected benefits**
- No Kafka to deploy or operate to run Microcks in full mode.
- Same communication model between the minions and the app whatever the deployment mode.
- Smaller footprint for the Uber distribution (nothing changes), and one less moving part for Kubernetes installations (Helm chart, operator, compose files).

**Design constraints we already identified**
- **No message persistence needed**: at startup (or reconnection), the minion already resynchronizes the services through the API. The pub/sub only has to carry live changes.
- **Ordering and no duplicates**: events of a given Service must be delivered in order, both through the replica pub/sub and in the fan-out to minions, with no duplicates. Note that topic ordering is only guaranteed per publisher, so the design likely needs a per-Service version or timestamp, with idempotent handling on the minion side.
- **Minion authentication** (full mode only): today the Kafka topics are not authenticated. The minion-to-webapp WebSocket must be authenticated when running in full mode (not needed in Uber, which runs without authentication). This is to be designed together with the replacement of Keycloak service accounts (see theme 3).
- **Event size**: events currently carry the whole service view; we may send lighter events and let the minion fetch the details.
- **Discovery and clustering** on Kubernetes: the mechanism already built for Reshapr can be reused.

**License check** 🔎
- The Hazelcast **core** (`com.hazelcast:hazelcast`, including `ITopic` and the Kubernetes discovery) is published under **Apache 2.0**. The SQL engine and some extensions are under the *Hazelcast Community License*, which is **not** OSI-approved and would not fit the CNCF policy: they would be excluded (and enforced in CI).
- Since 5.4, security fixes for the Community Edition are delivered with minor releases only, so we would have to follow them closely.
- To confirm with the CNCF, and to double-check the exact dependency tree.

**Alternatives considered**
- Use MongoDB change streams (requires a replica set, resume tokens handling) or PostgreSQL `LISTEN/NOTIFY` if a relational database were chosen.
- Let each minion connect to all replicas (headless service): simpler, but multiplies connections and complicates ordering and deduplication.
- Keep Kafka as an *optional* transport for those who already run it.

**Open points**
- 🔎 Hazelcast vs. other embedded pub/sub options, and the long-term risk linked to the vendor's Community/Enterprise model.
- 🔎 Exact ordering and deduplication scheme across replicas.
- 🔎 Authentication scheme for minions (internal API tokens, OIDC client credentials, mTLS).
- 🔎 Impact on the Helm chart, the operator and the existing installations (migration notes from Kafka).

## Questions for the community

1. Which of these themes matter most to you? What is missing?
2. **Database**: any strong reason to prefer PostgreSQL over MongoDB for your deployments? Any CNCF/legal input on the SSPL?
3. **Multi-tenancy**: how do you use Microcks today to separate teams, environments or mock variants?
4. **Authentication**: which identity providers do you need to support? Do you rely on Keycloak-specific features?
5. **Quarkus**: any concerns about the move, as a user or a contributor?
6. **Agents/MCP**: is this a direction you want Microcks to take, and with which first use case?
7. What are your hard backward-compatibility constraints (APIs, URLs, installation methods)?
8. **Kafka**: do you deploy Microcks in full mode today? Would you be happy to drop the Kafka dependency, or do you rely on the provided Kafka for other purposes?
9. **Scaling**: how many webapp replicas and async minions do you run, and what are your constraints (network policies, service mesh, multi-cluster)?
10. **Embedded clustering**: any objection to embedding a clustering library in the webapp (footprint, security policies, licensing)?

Feel free to comment per theme, so that we can split the discussion into dedicated issues later.

## Outcome

Implement loopback ASP.NET Core mock process, static/stateful/dataset/script responses, captured examples, and OpenAPI examples.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Priority/specificity precedence and ambiguous/unknown matches are deterministic and diagnosable.
- [ ] Delay/error/termination/seeded intermittent-failure fixtures pass.
- [ ] External binding requires explicit configuration; desktop start never exposes the internet automatically.

## Specification and dependencies

- Product specification sections: 17–18.
- Current desktop target: Windows 11 x64. Headless support: Windows/Linux x64. ARM64 is deferred.
- Project: https://github.com/users/git-maniam/projects/4
- Tracking key: `P8.1`
- Parent phase: https://github.com/git-maniam/API-Wrangler/issues/33
- Depends on: https://github.com/git-maniam/API-Wrangler/issues/30

## Delivery policy

Move to In progress before implementation. Keep acceptance checkboxes and verification evidence current. Move to In review only when a reviewable PR exists. Done requires verified acceptance and merged changes; never equate local code or a cross-build with release completion.

Implementation plan tracking; no due date is implied by priority or size.
