## Earlier request, reviews and evidence

## Outcome and current basis

Implement `spoke-sh/spoke` in **this repository**, developing against mocked service endpoints while Spoke Platform's management APIs are built. The immediate deliverable is a real Terraform Plugin Framework provider whose HTTP client and lifecycle behavior work against a local, stateful test server. Mock results establish provider behavior against a proposed contract; they do not establish that a platform service exists.

This is the implementation tracker for this repository. It carries forward [Transit #290](https://github.com/spoke-sh/transit/issues/290) with the ownership, independent versioning, and distribution corrections in `HANDOFF.md` in the provider checkout. The older issue remains historical context.

Inspected basis:

- Provider local commit `51f215429c086f335ae137e6bbf80dd455fd42f3` (not yet on remote `main` at inspection): locked Nix shell, five public Just tasks, CI, development instructions, and handoff are present. No Go module, resources, or mock endpoints exist yet.
- Platform `78cebeb173916810c107d6a90ed5711f63f4d742`: [contracts](https://github.com/spoke-sh/platform/blob/78cebeb173916810c107d6a90ed5711f63f4d742/docs/platform-contracts.md) explicitly describe missing tenant provisioning and deployment APIs. [Milestones 4–6](https://github.com/spoke-sh/platform/blob/78cebeb173916810c107d6a90ed5711f63f4d742/docs/roadmap/README.md) still own artifacts, workloads, and customer data. The inspected checkout has no published OpenAPI specification for these management operations.

The provider owns Terraform adaptation; platform owns product policy and provisioning; Transit owns reusable runtime primitives. Do not implement the service backend in this repository.

## Decisions for implementation

- Use Go, Terraform Plugin Framework, protocol 6, and independently pinned framework/testing dependencies. Retain the existing Nix toolchain unless dependency compatibility requires an explicit update.
- Use the real HTTP client in both mock and live tests. Configure its endpoint through ordinary provider configuration. Do not add a production `mock` mode or CRUD implementations that fabricate state without calling the API.
- Use Go's [`net/http/httptest`](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/httptest) for a local HTTP/TLS server with isolated state per test. No Docker, AWS, Transit runtime, or external mock service is required for the initial test lane.
- Exercise the provider with a real Terraform CLI through [`terraform-plugin-testing`](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/testing/acceptance-tests). Terraform's provider-level mocking would bypass the implementation we need to test.
- Start with project/environment discovery and **`spoke_bucket`** CRUD. Seed its parent scopes in the fixture. Buckets exercise import, drift, asynchronous operations, retained data, and dependency-restricted deletion without needing a workload runtime.
- Treat resource names, routes, payloads, and authentication below as **proposed test contracts** until the platform owner publishes a supported version. Mock-only resources remain experimental and must not be advertised as supported platform services.

## 1. Scaffold the provider

- [ ] Add root `go.mod`, `go.sum`, and `main.go`, using module path `github.com/spoke-sh/terraform-provider-spoke` and provider address `registry.terraform.io/spoke-sh/spoke`.
- [ ] Implement provider metadata, schema validation, and protocol-6 serving in `internal/provider/`. Pin dependency versions compatible with the locked Go compiler.
- [ ] Define endpoint, explicit organization/project/environment target assertions, externally supplied machine credentials, TLS trust, and bounded operation timeouts. Prefer environment/file credential sources; no credentials in resource attributes or examples.
- [ ] Permit custom test CA trust without disabling TLS verification. Reject missing/invalid configuration, unknown required values at apply, incompatible target scopes, and unsupported endpoint schemes before mutation.
- [ ] Establish `internal/platformclient/`, `internal/testutil/mockplatform/`, and fixtures under `testdata/`. Add only implemented resources to provider registration.
- [ ] Remove missing-`go.mod` success paths from `just check` and the CI build condition once the scaffold lands; missing source should then fail CI.

**Exit:** `just build` produces the provider; schema/configuration tests pass; Terraform can negotiate the provider protocol without contacting a platform service during validation.

## 2. Specify the draft boundary and build the mock server

Publish a small, versioned draft OpenAPI/schema fixture in `testdata/contracts/`, with a README naming its provisional status, source basis, and unresolved platform decisions. Record a capability matrix: operation, scope, authentication, IDs, request/response, error codes, revision checks, operation recovery, deletion semantics, and owner. When a platform-owned schema exists, pin it and generate boundary types from that source.

These route shapes are **illustrative fixture routes, not existing platform endpoints**. Confirm them in the draft before implementation:

| Capability | Proposed fixture surface |
| --- | --- |
| Target and supported capabilities | Authenticated read of target identity and API capabilities |
| Project discovery | `GET /v1/projects`, `GET /v1/projects/{project_id}` |
| Environment discovery | `GET /v1/projects/{project_id}/environments[/{environment_id}]` |
| First managed collection | `GET/POST {environment_scope}/buckets` |
| First managed object | `GET/PATCH/DELETE {environment_scope}/buckets/{bucket_id}` |
| Original-operation inspection | `GET {scope}/operations/{operation_id}` |
| Recovery before Terraform received an ID | Authorized operation lookup by durable management key and operation generation within `{scope}` |

Here `{environment_scope}` is the explicit project/environment path and `{scope}` is the operation's authorized ownership scope. Final route names, import syntax, and success/error envelopes are contract decisions.

- [ ] Define opaque immutable IDs separately from names, desired revisions, active revisions, operation IDs, and physical instances.
- [ ] Specify synchronous reads and asynchronous mutation acceptance, settlement, terminal failures, cancellation/timeouts, and authoritative absence.
- [ ] Define stable management key + request fingerprint + operation generation, duplicate replay, conflicting payload rejection, authorized pending-operation discovery, receipt retention, and ownership conflicts between Terraform states. A later legitimate return to an old configuration must be a new operation, not an accidental replay.
- [ ] Use synthetic scoped credentials in fixtures; proposed bearer authentication is a test assumption until platform automation auth is confirmed. Test authentication separately from resource authorization.
- [ ] Implement strict routing, request validation, pagination, revision preconditions, structured errors, and a concurrency-safe resource/operation store.
- [ ] Fail tests on unexpected requests. Provide test-only Go controls to seed scopes/data, advance operations, change observed state, revoke access, and inject failures; do not expose these controls as proposed public API endpoints.
- [ ] Keep operation progression independent of read requests. Polling observes state; the fixture's scheduler/test controller causes transitions.
- [ ] Use deterministic IDs, injected clocks/backoff, explicit synchronization, and bounded timeouts. Avoid arbitrary sleeps and shared global state.
- [ ] Test the fixture itself with raw HTTP requests and golden JSON/schema examples. Do not reuse the provider's lifecycle/retry logic in the fake: client and fake agreeing on the same bug is not contract evidence.

**Exit:** fixture contract tests cover success, denial, revision conflict, duplicate submission, operation lookup, pagination, and protected deletion. The fixture never contacts a cloud account. Missing platform contract decisions are explicit rather than inferred from UI surfaces.

## 3. Implement and verify the platform HTTP client

- [ ] Implement typed requests/responses with an injectable `http.Client`, credential source, clock, and retry policy. Validate response identity, scope, payload shape, and supported contract version.
- [ ] Bound individual requests, response sizes, pages, polling intervals, and total settlement time. Propagate context cancellation.
- [ ] Retry safe reads on eligible transient failures with bounded backoff and server retry hints. Mutating retries must preserve the original recoverable identity and preconditions; ambiguous transport failures must not issue fresh creates.
- [ ] Preserve typed errors: invalid input, unauthenticated, forbidden, authoritative not-found, stale revision, idempotency conflict, quota, dependency conflict, unavailable, and uncertain outcome.
- [ ] Treat generic/masked 404s, unsupported routes, and incomplete listings separately from authoritative absence. A read denial must never silently remove an object from Terraform state.
- [ ] Redact credentials and sensitive payloads from diagnostics/request recordings; prevent credential forwarding across unapproved redirects.
- [ ] Cover TLS verification, malformed/oversized replies, partial pagination, rate limiting, timeouts, and lost acceptance replies against the mock server.

**Exit:** client tests verify observable HTTP requests and responses, including unchanged mutation identity across retries, rather than only mocked client method calls.

## 4. Deliver the first Terraform lifecycle against mocks

- [ ] Add project/environment data sources and `spoke_bucket`, with scope IDs, a durable non-secret management key, mutable display name, contract-backed settings, explicit deletion protection, computed stable ID/revision, and operation timeouts. Only add fields justified by the draft contract.
- [ ] Define one canonical, scope-qualified import format and verify imported identity against the selected scope. Do not adopt an unrelated object by matching its name.
- [ ] Keep planning, refresh, and discovery observational. Reads may inspect operation status but must not submit mutations, build artifacts, or advance reconciliation.
- [ ] Implement create/read/update/delete/import using the same client used for a live endpoint. Preserve known IDs and operation references on failure; private state is additional recovery evidence, not the only pre-dispatch journal.
- [ ] Add real Terraform plan/apply/refresh/import/update/destroy tests through protocol-6 provider factories and the local HTTP fixture. Trust the fixture CA through the normal client configuration.
- [ ] Assert the happy path has an empty second plan, names can change without changing stable IDs, drift is detected, import agrees with configuration, and destroy removes only the intended object.
- [ ] Inspect both Terraform state and the mock server's operation/resource records. A passing Terraform state assertion alone cannot prove the intended request occurred.

**Exit:** a documented example completes the full bucket lifecycle locally and in credential-free CI. An unplanned mutation during plan/refresh fails the test. This is explicitly labeled mock-backed provider qualification.

## 5. Prove uncertainty, isolation, and data protection

Run these scenarios against the first resource before copying its patterns to other resources:

| Scenario | Required observation |
| --- | --- |
| Create accepted, reply lost | Retry discovers the original operation and creates exactly one logical resource |
| Provider killed before returning an ID | Restart with the same configuration/management key recovers the original resource |
| Interrupted update/delete or lost terminal reply | Original operation remains inspectable; timeout does not claim rollback |
| Later return to an earlier configuration | New operation generation is distinguishable from replay |
| Concurrent applies and stale revisions | Conflict is reported; no silent last-writer overwrite or second-state takeover |
| Permission revoked or cross-tenant target | No disclosure/mutation; denied reads preserve state |
| Renamed object and same-name recreation | Rename preserves ID; recreation has a new ID and is not silently adopted |
| Nonempty/protected bucket or dependent binding | Delete is refused; no implicit force-empty/cascade |
| Rate limit, quota refusal, outage, malformed response, incomplete page | Bounded error path; no false absence or successful completion |
| Operation remains pending beyond timeout | Diagnostic retains recovery context; accepted work is not duplicated |
| Secret-bearing failure response | No secret bytes appear in state, saved plans, logs, or diagnostics |

- [ ] Use a **separate provider process** for crash tests. In-process provider factories alone cannot establish process-death recovery.
- [ ] Keep the fixture server/operation ledger alive across provider restarts. For server restart cases, persist only synthetic fixture state in a test temporary directory and verify replay.
- [ ] Make fault points deterministic: before dispatch, after accepted intent is stored, before an HTTP reply, and after completion but before the provider records it.
- [ ] Verify unrelated data/resources survive every cleanup path. Cleanup targets only known fixture identities and must not erase evidence before assertions.

**Exit:** every case above has executable assertions; crash tests prove absence of duplicate logical resources. These tests validate the proposed recovery protocol, not real platform durability.

## 6. Expand the service graph in dependency order

Keep this as separate reviewable resource slices, reusing the tested client/operation helpers but keeping service-specific schemas explicit:

| Slice | Resources / reads | Extra behavior to specify and mock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope and access | `spoke_project`, `spoke_environment`, `spoke_service_account`, `spoke_grant` | Ownership, parent deletion restrictions, scoped access, revocation; credential issuance remains outside state |
| Artifacts and data | `spoke_artifact_registry`, `spoke_database`, expand `spoke_bucket`; matching reads | Registry retention/immutable digests, database profile/capacity/retention, data protection |
| Workload connections | `spoke_secret_reference`, `spoke_service_binding` | References only, exact dependency IDs, binding does not implicitly grant access |
| Containers and ingress | `spoke_container_service`, `spoke_endpoint`; matching reads | Immutable image digest, desired/active revision, health, private/public routing, dependency-safe teardown |

- [ ] Add each API operation to the draft contract and fixture before its provider resource.
- [ ] For every resource, require lifecycle/import/empty-plan tests plus denial, revision conflict, interruption, and its deletion rules.
- [ ] Exercise the combined mocked journey: scope → scoped identity → registry/database/bucket → container and binding → endpoint → digest update → revoke → retire compute while retaining separately owned data.
- [ ] Keep image build/push, object file transfer, database rows, and individual container instances outside ordinary managed-resource lifecycle. Do not pretend management mocks implement OCI, S3, or a database data plane.

Jobs/schedules, queues/streams, volumes, custom domains, backups/clones, scaling/placement, and bucket-object content resources remain later work with separate lifecycle contracts.

**Exit:** mock-tested coverage is listed per resource and draft contract revision. No unsupported real service is listed as delivered.

## Test commands and CI changes (planned in steps 2–4)

Keep five public recipes and the private default listing helper. The existing `test-acc` recipe currently assumes a real fixture; change its interface deliberately when introducing the mock lane:

| Command | Planned behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `just fmt` | Existing formatters, plus generated-artifact formatting when added |
| `just check` | Existing checks, Go vet/unit tests, and mock-backed Terraform acceptance |
| `just build` | Build the actual provider executable |
| `just test` | Unit/client/fixture tests with `TF_ACC` unset |
| `just test-acc` or `just test-acc mock` | Terraform acceptance against an automatically started local fixture |
| `just test-acc live` | Explicit real endpoint, isolated tenant, and external credentials; fail if required configuration is absent |

These are five recipes; `mock|live` is an argument to `test-acc`. Reject unknown modes. Never select live mode because credentials happen to exist in the environment, and never fall back from failed live tests to mocks. Select the two test suites explicitly so enabling `TF_ACC` for mock acceptance cannot execute live cases.

The testing harness runs the pinned Terraform binary via `TF_ACC_TERRAFORM_PATH`; `TF_ACC` is enabled only for the selected acceptance subprocess. See the [testing harness environment requirements](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/testing/acceptance-tests#requirements-and-recommendations).

Normal PR CI must need no platform/cloud credentials or remote state. After dependency acquisition, mock tests communicate only with loopback fixtures and use local Terraform state. CI must fail on missing Terraform, zero selected acceptance tests, or skipped required cases. Keep live qualification in an explicit separately authorized workflow, and label mock, process-recovery, installed-consumer, and live evidence separately.

Start execution on Linux amd64, evaluate the existing four Nix systems, and add actual Linux arm64/macOS execution gates before advertising those platforms. Test the chosen minimum Terraform version (initial candidate `1.10`) and the pinned current version before publishing a compatibility claim.

## 7. Package and test an installed consumer

- [ ] Add `buildGoModule` with verified `vendorHash`, `packages.<system>.terraform-provider-spoke`, and a versioned filesystem mirror once the provider builds.
- [ ] Preserve generated schema inputs in Nix source filters. Keep evaluation/build/shell entry free of deployment effects and secrets.
- [ ] Add a clean external-consumer fixture with a pinned provider flake/release, scoped `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE`, and checked `.terraform.lock.hcl`. Run init without backend credentials, then the lifecycle against the external mock server using the built provider executable.
- [ ] Use normal mirror/version/checksum selection, not `dev_overrides`, for installation evidence. Exclude only this provider from direct registry lookup while it is mirror-only.
- [ ] Generate provider/resource docs and examples; clearly mark experimental mock-only coverage.
- [ ] Use independent SemVer and immutable artifact identities. Mirror and registry bytes must match for the same version; source-built artifacts need a distinct prerelease identity when bytes differ.

**Exit:** another repository can install the exact provider and exercise the mocked slice without source-tree imports or development overrides. The consumer does not compile the provider.

## 8. Reconcile with real platform endpoints and qualify release

Platform contract work proceeds alongside steps 1–7; do not wait until the end to review draft assumptions. Before promoting a resource to supported:

- [ ] Resolve the platform-owned management API, automation auth, scoped IDs, errors, revisions, asynchronous settlement, recovery-key generations/retention, dependency deletion, and service-specific guarantees.
- [ ] Replace the provisional specification with the published schema/version. Run the same applicable contract/lifecycle scenarios against an isolated live platform fixture, with backend-specific setup kept in the test harness.
- [ ] Report divergences explicitly and update client, fixtures, schemas, tests, and docs together. Do not weaken a fake merely to make provider tests green.
- [ ] Re-run interrupted operations and authorization/data-protection scenarios against the real backend.
- [ ] Independently qualify registry push/pull, bucket upload/download, database access, workload data access, and endpoint reachability. Management-state agreement does not establish data-plane functionality.
- [ ] Publish exact provider/platform/API revisions, tested Terraform versions and operating systems, independent release artifacts, and the capability matrix.

**Exit:** the full initial service graph has live evidence, recovery preserves original accepted work, retained data survives compute teardown, and a clean external consumer can install the published provider.

## First implementation checkpoint

Complete steps **1–4** for one bucket plus scope discovery, with draft contract tests and a mandatory mock-backed CI lane. Add the failure cases in step 5 before expanding the resource inventory. Packaging can proceed once that slice builds; production-support claims remain gated by step 8.

This issue is a plan. It does not implement endpoints, create platform resources, or qualify a live service.
title: Implement the Spoke Terraform provider with mocked service endpoints

body:
### Problem & Solution Overview

Users want to set listening times freely: "play my preset on Tuesday and Friday to Sunday at 14:44 and switch off after 47 minutes with a fade-out" must work exactly as well as "a 47 minute sleep timer". Today:

| Wish | Sleep timer (#537) | Scheduled actions (#543) |
|---|---|---|
| Countdown of 47 min with fade-out, then stop or standby | ✅ duration 1–720 min (custom value), fade 0–300 s, end action stop/standby | – |
| Start a preset at 14:44 on chosen weekdays (or once) | – | ✅ weekdays + time, `play_preset`, optional volume + fade-in |
| **Start at 14:44 and switch off 47 min later with a fade-out** | – | ❌ only possible with two separate schedules, and the scheduled `stop`/`standby` has **no fade-out** |
| **Switch off at a clock time (e.g. 23:30) with a fade-out** | – | ❌ `stop`/`standby` is abrupt (no `VolumeFader`) |
| Enter "1 h 30 min" instead of 90 minutes | ❌ UI: presets + minutes only | – |
| Source other than a preset (AUX, Bluetooth) | – | ❌ out of scope in #543 (separable item 1, depends on #556) |

**Solution:** extend the schedules of #543 with an optional **end phase** that reuses the sleep timer, add an optional **fade-out** to scheduled `stop`/`standby`, and let the UI take durations as **hours + minutes**. No new scheduler, no new device calls: the end phase is `SleepTimerService.start(...)` armed by the runner, the fade-out reuses `VolumeFader`.

### User stories
- As a user I want my speaker to start preset 2 every Tuesday and Friday–Sunday at 14:44 and to fade out and switch to standby 47 minutes later.
- As a user I want a speaker to fade out and switch off at 23:30 every day instead of cutting off abruptly.
- As a user I want to enter a sleep timer or an end time as "1 h 30 min".

### Decisions (already made — do not re-open)
- **Depends on #543 (A1 and A2 merged) and #537 (merged) and #535.** Do not start until `apps/backend/src/opencloudtouch/schedules/` (repository, runner) and `sleep_timer/` exist on `main`; if they are absent, stop and comment on this issue. The shared pieces come from #537: `VolumeFader`, `devices/playback.py`, `SleepTimerService`.
- **Source = what #543 can start.** "A certain source" today means preset slot 1–6 of each selected device. The end phase is defined for the *start action* in general, so it applies automatically to a later `select_source` action (AUX/Bluetooth, separable item of #543 / #556) without another change. Sources other than presets stay out of scope here.
- **Delivery: two PRs.** **A** (backend: fields, validation, runner, tests, OpenAPI, docs) then **B** (frontend, after A). If #543 A1 is not yet merged when this issue is picked up, fold the new columns into its `CREATE TABLE`; otherwise add them with `_apply_migration` in the range **450–474** reserved by #543 (one `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` statement per migration; defaults keep existing rows valid).
- **End phase = sleep timer.** After a `play_preset` run succeeded on a device and `end_after_minutes` is set, the runner calls `SleepTimerService.start(device_id, end_after_minutes, end_fade_seconds, end_action)` for that device. The timer is persisted by #537, so it survives a restart; cancelling it (`DELETE /api/devices/{id}/sleep-timer`) works as usual; a later schedule run or a manual timer replaces it (one timer per device).
- **Fade-out on stop/standby.** A scheduled `stop` or `standby` gets `fade_out_seconds` (0–300, default 0 = abrupt as today). With a value > 0 the device is handled like the end of a sleep timer: if it is not playing → `skipped`/`already_stopped` (or `already_standby`); else read `V0`; if `V0 > 0` and not muted, fade `V0 → 0` over `fade_out_seconds` with `VolumeFader` (a manual volume change during the fade aborts without stopping and the run is `success` with `detail="manual_change"`); then `stop_playback` (and `POWER` after 1 s for `standby` unless already in standby) and restore `V0` best effort. The per-device budget of #543 excludes the fade; the fade is bounded by `fade_out_seconds + 30 s`.
- **Failure to arm the end phase.** If the start succeeded but `SleepTimerService.start` fails after the #543 retry policy (1 + 3 retries, 20 s apart), the run ends `failed` with `error_code = "end_not_armed"` (playback keeps running; documented, because the user would otherwise not notice that the speaker will not switch off).
- **No wall-clock end time in the end phase.** An "until 15:31" end is expressed by a second schedule with action `stop`/`standby` and `fade_out_seconds` (this issue); the end phase only takes a duration.
- **Hours/minutes entry is a UI concern.** The API keeps minutes (`duration_minutes`, `end_after_minutes`: 1–720); the UI converts. No API change for the sleep timer.
- **Defaults:** `end_after_minutes = null` (no end phase), `end_fade_seconds = 30`, `end_action = "stop"`, `fade_out_seconds = 0`. Existing schedules behave exactly as before.

---

## Part A — Backend

### A.1 Data and contract
New fields on the schedule object of #543 (request, response, `PUT` full replacement):
- `end_after_minutes: int | null` — 1–720; only with `action == "play_preset"`.
- `end_fade_seconds: int = 30` — 0–300; only meaningful with `end_after_minutes`.
- `end_action: "stop" | "standby" = "stop"` — only meaningful with `end_after_minutes`.
- `fade_out_seconds: int = 0` — 0–300; only with `action` `stop` or `standby`.

Not applicable fields must be at their default (otherwise `schedule_invalid_combination`), as in #543. Validation (422, `errors[].path` + `code`, all violations returned together, new codes added to `core/error_codes.py` and the OpenAPI codes list):
- `schedule_invalid_end_after` (`end_after_minutes` outside 1–720)
- `schedule_invalid_end_fade` (`end_fade_seconds` outside 0–300) and `schedule_end_fade_too_long` (`end_fade_seconds > end_after_minutes * 60`, path `end_fade_seconds`)
- `schedule_invalid_end_action` (`end_action` not `stop`/`standby`)
- `schedule_invalid_fade_out` (`fade_out_seconds` outside 0–300)
- `schedule_invalid_combination` (end fields with `stop`/`standby`; `fade_out_seconds` with `play_preset`)

`next_run_at` and `last_run` are unchanged; `last_run.error_code` may now be `end_not_armed`. Run `detail`/`error_code` additions: `end_not_armed` (failure), `already_stopped`/`already_standby` (existing skips).

### A.2 Runner behaviour
- `play_preset` with `end_after_minutes`: after the preset press (and the optional fade-in finished or aborted), arm the sleep timer for that device. The end of the fade-in and the start of the timer do not overlap: the timer starts when the fade-in has finished (so its duration counts from "playback is at its target volume"). A fade-in aborted by a manual volume change still arms the timer.
- `stop`/`standby` with `fade_out_seconds > 0`: as in "Decisions". Shutdown cancels a running fade-out within 3 s and restores `V0` best effort (same rule as the sleep timer shutdown).
- Interaction with an active sleep timer: the `play_preset` run first cancels an existing timer (#543); the newly armed timer replaces nothing afterwards. A scheduled `stop`/`standby` with fade-out also cancels an active sleep timer of that device first.
- Everything else (idempotency key, missed runs, per-device lock, retries, history, `POST /run`) is unchanged.

### A.3 Acceptance criteria — Backend (fake clock, stateful mock device, in-memory or temp-file stores)
1. **Given** a schedule `Tue, Fri, Sat, Sun` (weekdays `[1,4,5,6]`) 14:44, `play_preset 2`, `end_after_minutes 47`, `end_fade_seconds 30`, `end_action standby` on a mock device, **when** the fake clock reaches Friday 14:44, **then** one run row per device is `success`, `PRESET_2` was pressed, a sleep timer with `duration_minutes 47`, `fade_seconds 30`, `end_action standby` exists for the device, and on Monday and Wednesday nothing fires.
2. **Given** the clock advances 47 minutes after the start, **then** the volume fades to 0 following the `VolumeFader` formula, the device is paused, the volume is restored and the device is in standby (the sleep timer sequence of #537, asserted end to end).
3. **Given** `play_preset` without `end_after_minutes`, **then** no sleep timer is created (behaviour of #543 unchanged) and an existing schedule row without the new columns still loads with the defaults.
4. **Given** `stop` with `fade_out_seconds 60` on a playing device, **then** volume calls follow the fader formula to 0, then `PAUSE`, then the volume is restored to `V0`; `standby` additionally presses `POWER` after 1 s unless the device is in standby; a device that is not playing → `skipped`/`already_stopped`; muted or `V0 == 0` → no fade, abrupt stop; a manual volume change during the fade → no stop, run `success`/`manual_change`.
5. **Given** `fade_out_seconds 0`, **then** `stop`/`standby` behave exactly as before this issue (regression).
6. **Given** `SleepTimerService.start` raises `DeviceConnectionError` on every attempt after a successful start, **then** the run is `failed`/`end_not_armed`, playback keeps running and 4 attempts were made 20 s apart.
7. **Given** an active manual sleep timer, **when** the scheduled start runs, **then** the old timer is cancelled before any `set_volume` and the new one replaces it; **given** a restart after the run, the armed timer still fires (persisted by #537).
8. **Given** each validation code of A.1, **then** a test asserts status 422, `errors[].path` and `code`; end fields with `stop`/`standby` and `fade_out_seconds` with `play_preset` give `schedule_invalid_combination`; `PUT` replaces the new fields; defaults apply when omitted.
9. Works with `OCT_MOCK_MODE=true` (stateful mock); all time-dependent tests use the fake clock; `openapi.yaml` updated (fields, codes); `docs/CONFIGURATION.md` section "Schedules" extended (end phase, fade-out, `end_not_armed`, "until a clock time = second schedule", sources other than presets are out of scope); `CHANGELOG.md` entry.

---

## Part B — Frontend (after A)

Extends `pages/Schedules.tsx` / the schedule form of #543 and `components/SleepTimer.tsx` of #537. Visual design comes from the designer; behaviour is mandatory.

### B.1 Functional requirements
1. **Duration input as hours + minutes** (new small component `DurationInput`, used by both): two number inputs "hours" (0–12) and "minutes" (0–59) with a combined total of 1–720 minutes; it shows the total ("= 1 h 47 min") and an inline error for 0 and for more than 720 minutes. In the sleep timer it sits next to the presets (presets stay; "Custom…" shows `DurationInput`); in the schedule form it is used for `end_after_minutes`. The wire value is the total in minutes.
2. **Schedule form — end phase:** for action `play_preset` an optional switch "Switch off after a duration": `DurationInput`, fade-out (off, 10 s, 30 s, 60 s; default 30 s; options longer than the duration are disabled), end action (stop / standby). Hidden and not sent for other actions or when the switch is off.
3. **Schedule form — fade-out for stop/standby:** for action `stop`/`standby` a fade-out select (off, 10 s, 30 s, 60 s, 120 s; default off). Hidden and not sent for `play_preset`.
4. **List and history:** the action summary shows the end phase ("Preset 2 · switches off after 47 min (standby, 30 s fade-out)") and the fade-out of stop/standby; `error_code` `end_not_armed` has a translated message ("The speaker started, but the switch-off timer could not be set — it may keep playing").
5. **Server errors** map by `path` + `code` (`getFieldErrors`): `schedule_end_fade_too_long` at the fade control, `schedule_invalid_end_after` at the duration, the other new codes as form-level messages.

### B.2 Accessibility
`DurationInput` is a labelled group (`role="group"`, visible legend), both inputs labelled, errors associated (`aria-invalid`, `aria-describedby`), the total is in a polite `role="status"` region (announced on change after a short debounce, not per keystroke).

### B.3 Acceptance criteria — Frontend
1. **Given** hours 0 and minutes 47, **then** the request carries `end_after_minutes: 47`; hours 1 and minutes 30 carries 90; 0 h 0 min, 12 h 1 min and non-integer values show an inline error and send nothing.
2. **Given** action `play_preset` with the end switch on, **then** `end_after_minutes`, `end_fade_seconds` and `end_action` are sent; with the switch off or another action, none of the end fields is in the body; `stop` sends `fade_out_seconds` only when chosen.
3. **Given** a 1-minute duration, **then** fade options longer than 60 s are disabled; a server `schedule_end_fade_too_long` shows the translated message at the fade control.
4. **Given** the sleep timer with "Custom…", **then** `DurationInput` is used, the remembered default (`oct.sleepTimer.defaults.duration`, minutes) is restored into hours/minutes, and the PUT body is unchanged from #537.
5. **Given** a run with `end_not_armed`, **then** the history shows the translated warning; an unknown code falls back to the generic text with the raw code.
6. All new strings in the 10 locales (`de, en, es, fr, it, ja, nl, pl, pt-BR, sv`, incl. `errors.api.<code>` for the new codes); Vitest tests for `DurationInput` (conversion, limits, a11y), the form's field visibility and request bodies; existing schedule and sleep timer tests still pass; Cypress `schedules.cy.ts` extended (create a schedule with an end phase → request body asserted via `cy.intercept`).

---

## Out of scope
- Sources other than presets (AUX, Bluetooth, arbitrary streams): separable items of #543, depend on #556. When `select_source` exists, the end phase applies to it by this issue's design (no further change expected, to be verified then).
- A wall-clock end time inside one schedule ("until 15:31"): use a second schedule with `stop`/`standby` and `fade_out_seconds`.
- Recurring sleep timers without starting playback (a schedule that only arms a timer).
- Per-schedule time zones, sunrise/sunset triggers, snooze, zone targets (#559).

## Assumptions to verify on real hardware (maintainers)
Same as #537 and #543 (PAUSE/STOP/POWER semantics, volume changes while paused, wake from standby, preset keys on Wave). Additionally: a fade-in that is still running when the end timer is armed is not expected to matter because the timer starts after the fade-in.

## Related issues
- Extends #543 "Scheduled actions (alarms)" and builds on #537 "Sleep timer"; depends on #535.
- Related: #556 (select source), #559 (saved groups) — not required.

---

## Definition of Ready

- [x] Problem, user story and originating request are described; scope and out of scope are explicit
- [x] Affected modules are named (⚙️ backend, 🖥️ frontend → 🔗 full-stack) and the work is split into two ordered PRs (backend, then frontend); the label `spec` is set
- [x] Acceptance criteria are testable (Given/When/Then), cover error paths and edge cases, and backend and frontend have separate, matching criteria
- [x] API contract, data model, mock-mode behaviour and claims about existing code are specified; claims about #537/#543 were checked against the issue texts (those modules are not on `main` yet, which is why the prerequisite rule applies)
- [x] Frontend part states functional requirements only (states, i18n, accessibility); visual design is not blocking
- [x] Test strategy is defined; hardware-dependent items are listed as assumptions with a named verifier (the maintainers)
- [x] Security, privacy and risk are considered (trusted-LAN model; no new network access, no new secrets; the end phase can switch a speaker off unexpectedly — opt-in per schedule)
- [x] Dependencies and ordering are stated ("do not start until #543 A1/A2 and #537 are merged"); no open questions remain; documentation impact is identified
- [ ] Reviewed by a second person or independent reviewers and their findings are incorporated

## Definition of Done (verifiable)

Each applicable item of `docs/DEFINITION_OF_DONE.md` is covered by an acceptance criterion above or by the following:
- Contracts: `apps/backend/openapi.yaml` updated, `npm run generate:api` run and committed; errors use `ErrorDetail` with stable codes
- Data/config: new columns via `CREATE TABLE` (if #543 A1 is unmerged) or `_apply_migration` in 450–474 with an upgrade test from the #543 schema; no new `OCT_*` variable
- UI: all new strings in every locale; loading, error and offline states unchanged or covered; keyboard operation and accessible names; phone-width layout
- Security/privacy: inputs validated, no secrets or tokens in logs; trusted-LAN model
- Documentation: "Schedules" section extended in `docs/CONFIGURATION.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, README feature list
- Deployment: n/a — no Docker/Compose/multi-arch impact
- Tests: unit and integration tests as listed, deterministic (fake clock), the feature works in mock mode, coverage of new/changed code ≥ 80 % (backend and frontend)
- CI: tests, lint, security scan, licence check, commit lint and the SonarCloud gate are green; Conventional Commits
- Review: a reviewer other than the author verifies the checklist; hardware-dependent behaviour is verified on a device or listed in the PR under "Open verifications and follow-ups" with a named owner
- ADR: n/a — extends existing domains

---

## Cross-cutting requirements

Apply the cross-cutting requirements of #543 and #537 unchanged (error contract with `code`, `raise_coded`, `errors[].path`, status conventions, backend/frontend conventions, i18n in all 10 locales, test and gate commands, docs, security model). Prerequisites: if #543 A1/A2 or #537 are not on `main`, stop and comment on this issue; never re-implement them here.
title: [Spec]: Scheduled sessions — end a scheduled start after a duration with a fade-out, fade-out for scheduled stop, hours/minutes entry

The owner wants the **maximum verified end-to-end completion today**. Do not convert proposed milestones into "passed" without durable evidence. Preserve the original hackathon deadline/fallbacks and submit only after approval.

**Baseline checked:** main `bc16065bae17be1e96f29f16cd20ae66b2c8e3a8`; backend [PR #21](../pull/21) exact head `02bcb6bc96b5d061a4b59fd51e035aaa92e641f3` Linux/Windows CI successful (run 41188568484), independent/merge and hosted acceptance outstanding; science [PR #23](../pull/23) CI green (run 41182295330), genuine G3 attempt **broker_failed** after `EMPTY_MODEL_RESPONSE` (finish_reason=length, reasoning exhausted 800-token cap). Keep existing G2/G3 evidence immutable; never let sealed gold material into model requests. body:
## Direction: Rift as an AI-operable mock engine

This epic is the first step of a larger direction (owner, 2026-11-03): imposters and stubs are increasingly going to be **written by AI agents, not by developers**, at the moment a test or simulation needs them — a stateful twin of a downstream service generated from its API spec, loaded into Rift minutes later, driven under precise control of its behaviour, time and randomness, and thrown away or re-generated as the hypothesis changes. Everything in this epic is what that requires and Rift lacks today:

| Agent-authored mocks need | This epic provides |
|---|---|
| to run code nobody reviewed for *safety*, only for *behaviour* | a real capability boundary (#1751) and a trust gate that does not require `--allowInjection` (#1752) |
| to be bounded no matter how wrong they are | pre-emptive deadline, memory cap, fuel budget per call (#1751) |
| control over time and randomness from the test or simulation side | virtual clock and seed per imposter (#1754, #1755, #1756) |
| hot replacement without a filesystem or a restart | content-addressed upload, pinned by hash (#1757) |
| to be the *same artifact* the agent unit-tests and the simulation drives | standard `wasi:http` components, extra exports tolerated (#1758) |
| a way to earn trust against the real service | `rift wasm check` over a recorded corpus (#1759) |

Later steps in this direction (not in this epic): an agent-facing surface for authoring and driving imposters (templates, structured feedback from `rift-lint`/`rift wasm check`, scenario control), and the simulation-runtime integration that consumes it.

## Why

Rift's two scripting engines, Rhai and JavaScript (Boa 0.22), are host code execution. `docs/features/scripting.md:54-57` says so: *"The code it admits runs with Rift's own privileges … Nothing below makes it a sandbox."* `--scripts-dir` confinement (#356) and the Rhai module disable (#1611) are hygiene, not isolation. Four consequences, each with its code path on master @ `5dc739a5`:

| Problem | Where |
|---|---|
| **No capability boundary.** A script can only be admitted from authors you would give a shell. Code written minutes ago by an AI agent, or a "twin" of a downstream service a test wants to run, cannot be loaded without that trust jump. | `--allowInjection` gate: `crates/rift-http-proxy/src/injection_gate.rs` |
| **Cooperative timeouts, no memory cap.** `_rift.script` runs on `spawn_blocking` under `tokio::time::timeout`; on elapse an abort flag is set. Rhai sees it via `on_progress`; Boa never does, so a runaway JS loop holds its blocking thread until Boa's iteration cap (10⁷) throws. Nothing bounds a script's memory. | `crates/rift-mock-core/src/scripting/bounded.rs:81-229`, `js_engine.rs:247` |
| **Not deterministic.** Flow-state TTLs read `SystemTime::now()` (6 sites in `backends/inmemory.rs`); Rhai `timestamp_header` reads `SystemTime`; Boa's `Date.now`/`Math.random` are stock; `_rift.fault` rolls use `rand::rng()`. A failing interaction cannot be replayed bit for bit, and a harness driving virtual time (ZIO `TestClock`, a simulation event loop) cannot move the mock's clock, so a 24 h TTL takes 24 h to test. | `handler.rs:2771-2808`, `rhai_engine.rs:144`, `template_fn.rs:382` |
| **State machines are awkward.** A collaborator that matters for what it does *over time* (sequence guard, dedupe window, promotion step) becomes a long untyped `ctx.state` script that cannot be unit-tested or reused outside Rift. | `_rift.script` + `FlowStore` |

A WebAssembly **component** engine under wasmtime fixes all four at once: the linker is the capability boundary, fuel + epoch + `StoreLimits` are pre-emptive and per call, `wasi:clocks`/`wasi:random` are host-virtualised (so determinism is a host setting, not a guest convention), and the artifact runs unchanged outside Rift.

Design note: `remote-vault/Rift-twin/Rift-WASM-engine-issue.md` (2026-11-03). This epic supersedes it where they differ.

## Decisions (2026-11-03, owner)

1. **Own flag `--allowWasm`, default on.** A component that passes the linker policy cannot execute host code, so it does not need `--allowInjection`. `--strict-wasm <hash-file>` later for pinned-hash-only mode (#1757).
2. **Deny by implementation, not by import list.** A hello-world Rust `wasm32-wasip2` component imports `wasi:cli/{environment,exit,stdin,stdout,stderr,terminal-*}`, `wasi:io/*`, `wasi:clocks/wall-clock`, `wasi:filesystem/{types,preopens}` without calling them (rust-lang/rust#150120). Refusing those imports would reject every real toolchain's output. So Rift *links* `wasi:cli`, `wasi:io`, `wasi:filesystem` (no preopens → every open fails), `wasi:clocks` and `wasi:random` (virtualised), and does **not** link `wasi:sockets/*` or `wasi:http/outgoing-handler`. A component importing an unlinked interface is refused at admission with the import named.
3. **Phase 1 is `_rift.script` only.** `engine` is honoured only there today (`imposter/types.rs:3936`); `inject`/`decorate`/predicate `inject` are Mountebank-JS surfaces. The wasm export mirrors `ScriptResult` (`pass | delay | reset | respond`), so one `respond` covers fault decisions and responses, as `_rift.script` does now.
4. **Per-request `Store` by default**, state only through the `rift:mock/state` host import (= `FlowStore`). `instance: "imposter"` is a phase-3 opt-in (#1758).
5. **The corpus is the saved imposter.** `GET /imposters/:port?replayable=true` already yields recorded stubs in order with recorded responses; `rift wasm check` reuses rift-verify's predicate→request synthesis. No new JSONL format.
6. **`step-actor` (simulation step mode) is not Rift's WIT.** Rift tolerates extra exports on a component; the simulation runtime owns its own package.
7. **Not a plug-in to `ScriptPool`.** `script_pool.rs`/`CompiledScript` are unused public code; the #1678 pool is `MbPool` in `js_engine.rs`, Boa-specific. The engine gets its own module `scripting/wasm/`.
8. **No new decode-time refusal anywhere.** `engine` stays `Option<String>` on the wire; unknown engines, missing components and bad imports are refused at admission (`stub_validator`) or at serve time, never inside `Deserialize` (rift-cluster replays stored bytes through `deserialize_replayed`).
9. **wasmtime 50.x** (latest 50.0.1, requires Rust 1.97; MSRV is 1.99), `wasmtime`/`wasmtime-wasi`/`wasmtime-wasi-http` on one major, bumped monthly with the rest of the deps (#1312 policy). Cargo feature `wasm`: default **on** in the `rift` binary, **off** in `rift-ffi` (measured +15.8 MB stripped).
10. **Spike-validated before implementation** (2026-11-03, vault `Rift-twin/wasm-spike/`, summary in the comment below): real `wasm32-wasip2` components against wasmtime 50 confirmed the sandbox policy, the pre-emptive deadline, determinism via WASI, the http export, and a per-request cost of 21–25 µs (3–5× faster than today's JS path). Corrections landed in #1751: fuel is unlimited by default, instance cap 16, `epoch_deadline_callback` + `UpdateDeadline::Yield`, limiter failures are not `Trap` values.

## Sub-issues

Phase 1 — engine, sandbox, limits
1. #1750 refactor: one `ScriptEngineKind` parsed in one place; retire `ScriptPool`/`CompiledScript`
2. #1751 `engine: "wasm"` — `rift:mock` components under wasmtime behind `_rift.script`, fuel/memory/epoch limits, `FlowStore` host import *(blocked by 1)*
3. #1752 `--allowWasm` (default on), separate from `--allowInjection`; `GET /config` reports `features` *(blocked by 2)*
4. #1753 `wasm` feature wiring: off in `rift-ffi`, on in the binary; binary-size delta recorded and documented *(blocked by 2)*

Phase 2 — deterministic time and randomness
5. #1754 per-imposter virtual clock: `PUT/GET/DELETE /imposters/{port}/clock`, `X-Rift-Now`; read by `wasi:clocks` and FlowStore TTLs *(blocked by 2)*
6. #1755 seeded randomness: `_rift.scriptEngine.seed` → `wasi:random`, `_rift.fault` rolls, template `random`; byte-identical replay test *(blocked by 2, 5)*
7. #1756 Rhai and JavaScript read the imposter clock and seed *(blocked by 5, 6)*

Phase 3 — hot load, http export, corpus check
8. #1757 content-addressed component registry: `POST/GET/DELETE /components`, `"component": "sha256:<hex>"`, `--datadir` persistence, `--strict-wasm` *(blocked by 2, 3)*
9. #1758 `export: "http"` serves `wasi:http/incoming-handler` components; `instance: "imposter"` *(blocked by 2)*
10. #1759 `rift wasm check` replays a saved imposter against a component offline *(blocked by 2; 5 for timestamps)*
11. #1760 wasm benches: cold compile, warm instantiate, warm call within 2× of JS *(blocked by 2)*

## Execution plan

| Batch | Issues | How |
|---|---|---|
| A | #1750 → #1751 → #1752 → #1753 | `/ship-issues` one at a time, in order |
| B (after A) | #1754 → #1755, then #1756 | `/ship-issues <n>` |
| C (after A; #1759 after #1754) | #1757, #1758 (Fable), #1759, #1760 | any order |

**Owner actions:** add `rustup target add wasm32-wasip2` to the CI matrix when #1751 lands (the example component is built from source); rotate the wasmtime major with the monthly dep bump.

**Downstream (filed at ship time, per `CLAUDE.local.md` 1f-cross, not now):**
- rift-java / rift-go / rift-node / rift-scala: `_rift.script` gains `component`, `export`, `knobs`, `instance`; `_rift.scriptEngine` gains `wasm`, `seed`, `clock`. Feature-detect by `features` containing `"wasm"` in `rift_build_info()` and the new `GET /config` `features` array; absence = engine too old. Their per-consumer key lists (#1343 gate) need the new keys.
- rift-cluster: opts into the `wasm` feature explicitly (`rift-http-proxy` is taken with `default-features = false`); the component registry is node-local, not Raft-replicated; `ADMIN_ROUTES` additions reach its OpenAPI automatically.
- `sdk-conformance/`: a wasm fixture only after all four SDKs adopt (it needs a `schemaVersion` bump).

## Definition of done

- [ ] `engine: "wasm"` works in `_rift.script` with `export: "rift"` and `export: "http"`.
- [ ] Sandbox negatives: a component importing `wasi:sockets/tcp` or `wasi:http/outgoing-handler` is refused at admission with the import named; `loop {}` returns a script timeout within `timeoutMs`; a 1 GiB allocation traps; after each the imposter still answers.
- [ ] With `seed` and a frozen clock, 20 replays of one request sequence give byte-identical responses and identical flow state.
- [ ] `FlowStore` is shared between a wasm stub and a Rhai stub on one imposter.
- [ ] One sha256 compiles once (trace counter); cold-compile / warm-instantiate / warm-call latency in benches; warm call within 2× of the JS `_rift.script` path.
- [ ] `rift-ffi` builds with and without `wasm`; the size delta is documented.
- [ ] `rift wasm check` passes on a saved imposter and fails with a per-field diff when one field is changed.
- [ ] A `wasi:http/proxy` component runs unchanged behind an imposter.
- [ ] Docs: a security-model page that says exactly what is and is not isolated.
title: epic(scripting): sandboxed engine "wasm" — WebAssembly components under wasmtime with pre-emptive limits and deterministic time

body:
## Problem

The contract mock is stateless: a `Responder` is synchronous, `(operation, request) => ContractResponse`, with no access to earlier requests. That is enough for Tier A and the recorder, but Tier B and Tier C (#295694, #295695) run multi-step workflows and agent conversations that create something and then read it back (post a message, then list the channel's history; create an issue, then get it). Sampled responses can't make the second step agree with the first, and plugging in a stateful backend (a generic store, or [vercel-labs/emulate](https://github.com/vercel-labs/emulate) for the few connectors it covers: Slack, Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, S3, Okta) isn't possible through the current signature.

## Proposal

- Change the seam now, while it has few callers: `Responder = (operation, request, context) => ContractResponse | Promise<ContractResponse>`, where `context` carries the mock's per-run state and a `next()` that falls through to the default chain (fixtures → recordings → examples → samples).
- Make the call sites async: `createResponseEngine`'s fallback, `withPagination`, the OpenAPI adapter and `createEmulatorFetch`.
- Every response still goes through response validation, so a stateful responder (or an external emulator behind it) is checked against the vendor spec like any other source.
- `reset()` clears responder state.
- A stateful responder itself (e.g. create/read/list/delete inferred from path templates) is out of scope until a Tier B case needs it.

## Acceptance

- Existing responders and tests keep working unchanged apart from the signature.
- A test responder that remembers a `POST` body and returns it on the matching `GET` works through `createEmulatorFetch`, and its responses are validated.
- An async responder works in-process and in server mode.

Part of #295699; follows #295684, used by #295694 and #295695.
title: [Connector validation][Emulator] Async, context-aware Responder for stateful responses

body:
## Why

`apic import spec.yaml` writes the requests, but until a backend exists there is nothing to run them against. `apic demo` is already a mock server shipped inside the binary; a spec-driven one generalises it and closes the import loop, so a frontend, an agent or a CI smoke run can proceed before the backend is written, and the course has an offline target for any spec.

The OpenAPI reader (`internal/openapi`) already resolves `$ref`, walks `responses` and derives a value from any schema (`exampleFromSchema`), and the demo API already routes with Go's `ServeMux` `{param}` patterns. A mock is the same walker pointed at responses, so this needs no new dependency and adds well under 0.5 % to the binary.

## Scope

`apic mock <openapi.yaml|openapi.json> [--port <port>]`:

- One route per operation, matching method and path; `{param}` path segments match anything.
- The response is the first 2xx declared, else `default`, else the first; a `2XX` key serves 200.
- The body comes from the media type's `example`, its first named `examples` entry, else a value derived from the schema, exactly as `import` builds request bodies. Response `headers` from the spec are set from their examples or schemas.
- `Prefer: code=404` picks another documented response and `Prefer: example=name` a named example (Prism's convention), so one request file can cover the error cases. An undocumented choice is a 406 with a JSON message.
- An unknown path is a 404 with a JSON message; a known path with the wrong method is the 405 `ServeMux` gives.
- Listens on `127.0.0.1` only, like `demo`; binds before printing, with the same timeouts and Ctrl-C shutdown. `--json` prints one startup object (the spec, the URL, the routes with the status each serves, `listening: true`) then keeps serving.
- A spec with no operations, or that is not OpenAPI 3, is an error with a catalogue code and exit 2.

## Not in scope

Stateful mocks, request validation, recording or proxying, and dynamic responses, latency or faults. Those are the rows the comparison page's "Deliberately not planned" table gains in #154, with the escape hatch for each. The course shows the command in #153.

## Checklist

- [ ] `internal/openapi/mock.go` builds an `http.Handler` and a route list from a document, with tests beside it (`mock_test.go`: default response, `Prefer`, class keys, headers, unknown path, bad spec)
- [ ] `internal/cli/mock.go`, sharing the listen-and-serve plumbing with `demo.go`; a test for the bad-port and bad-spec paths and the `--json` startup line
- [ ] a new code in `runner.Catalogue` for a spec the mock cannot serve, with its case in `internal/cli/errors_test.go`, and `CodeServer`'s entry naming `apic mock`; `task docs:errors`
- [ ] docs: a section in the site's `cli.md`, a line in `cheatsheet.md` (then `task skill`), `task docs:cli`, a mention in `skills/apic/SKILL.md` and in `docs/architecture.md`'s package list, and the README quick start
- [ ] `task check` green, binary size checked with `task build && ls -la bin/apic`
title: apic mock: serve an OpenAPI 3 document as a stateless mock API

body:
## 背景

API Schema Plannerにより、GitHub IssueからOpenAPI 3.1ベースのAPI Schema Proposalを生成し、人間がレビュー・承認できるようになった。

一方で、現状はAPI Schemaを承認した後に、その契約を使ってFrontendがRails APIの完成を待たずに開発できるMock Serverがない。

このままだとContract-FirstでAPI仕様を先に確定しても、Frontend / Backendの並行開発に十分つながらない。

そのため、**承認済みOpenAPIからローカルMock Serverを起動できる仕組み**を追加する。

---

## 目的

API Schema Plannerで承認されたOpenAPIをそのままMock APIとして利用できるようにし、Expo / React AdminがRails API完成前からAPI接続・画面実装を開始できるようにする。

```text
GitHub Issue
  ↓
API Schema Planner
  ↓
OpenAPI Proposal
  ↓
Human Review / Approval
  ↓
Mock Server
  ├─ Expo
  └─ React Admin

同時並行
  ↓
Rails API実装
```

---

## 基本方針

初期実装ではOpenAPI 3.1からMock Serverを起動できる既存ツールを利用する。

第一候補は **Prism** とする。

理由:

- OpenAPIからそのままMock Serverを起動できる
- 独自Mock APIを実装しなくてよい
- Contract-Firstの流れと相性がよい
- Frontend / Backendが同じOpenAPIを参照できる

ただし、実装時にPrismより適切な選択肢がある場合は比較のうえ変更してよい。

---

## 想定コマンド

例:

```bash
pnpm api:mock https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<number>
```

または責務上より自然であれば、以下のような形式でもよい。

```bash
pnpm api:mock --schema .harness/api-schema/<issue-number>/openapi.yaml
```

CLIインターフェースは実装時に確定する。

---

## Mock Server起動条件

未承認のAPI SchemaをFrontendが契約として利用しないようにする。

Issue URLを入力とする場合は、以下を確認する。

```text
planner:api-schema-status
        ↓
APPROVED ?
  ├─ No  → 起動しない
  └─ Yes → Mock Server起動
```

承認判定のSource of Truthは既存のAPI Schema Approvalとし、`api-schema-approved`ラベルだけを信用しない。

Mock Serverが使用するOpenAPIは、承認対象と同一digestのProposalであることを保証する。

---

## Mock APIの振る舞い

最低限以下を満たす。

- OpenAPIに定義されたpath / methodで応答できる
- response statusをOpenAPIから解釈できる
- response schemaに沿ったJSONを返せる
- array / object / enum / nullable等の基本schemaを扱える
- Cognito JWT必須endpointでも、ローカルMock用途として起動できる
- 実際のCognitoやRails APIへ接続しない
- Secret / Credentialの実値を要求・保存しない

認証必須endpointについては、初期段階では本物のJWT検証を行わず、Mock ServerとしてFrontend開発を妨げない方式とする。

必要であれば固定Bearer tokenや認証スキップ等を採用するが、**実Credentialは利用しない**。

---

## Frontendからの利用

Frontend側は環境変数等でAPI Base URLを切り替えられる前提とする。

例:

```text
Local Mock
http://localhost:4010

Development API
https://dev-api.example.com
```

Mock Server自身にExpo / React Admin固有のロジックは持たせない。

---

## OpenAPIとの関係

Mock Server用に別API仕様を持たない。

```text
Approved OpenAPI
      ↓
Mock Server
      ↓
Frontend

Approved OpenAPI
      ↓
Rails implementation
```

Frontend MockとRails APIが別々の契約を持つことを避け、**OpenAPIを共通Contractとして利用する**。

---

## 受け入れ要件

- [ ] 承認済みOpenAPIからローカルMock Serverを起動できる
- [ ] 未承認のAPI SchemaではMock Serverを起動しない
- [ ] `api-schema-approved`ラベルだけでは承認済みと判定しない
- [ ] 承認対象と同一digestのOpenAPIを利用する
- [ ] OpenAPI 3.1のpath / methodをMock APIとして提供できる
- [ ] OpenAPIのresponse schemaに沿ったJSONを返せる
- [ ] object / array / enum / nullableを最低限扱える
- [ ] Cognito JWT必須endpointをFrontend開発用にMockできる
- [ ] 本物のCognito / Rails API / Production APIへ接続しない
- [ ] Secret / Credential実値を必要としない
- [ ] FrontendからAPI Base URLを切り替えて利用できる設計にする
- [ ] Mock用の独自API仕様を持たずOpenAPIをSource of Truthにする
- [ ] 起動方法・利用方法をREADMEまたはdocsに記載する
- [ ] CI / Harnessの既存品質ゲートを壊さない

---

## 検証例

```text
Given API Schema ProposalがAPPROVEDである
When Mock Serverを起動する
Then OpenAPIに定義されたendpointへHTTPリクエストできる
And response schemaに沿ったJSONが返る
```

```text
Given API Schema Proposalが未承認である
When Mock Serverを起動しようとする
Then 起動を拒否する
And 未承認である理由を表示する
```

---

## 今回やらないこと

- Rails APIの自動実装
- Frontend API clientの自動生成
- OpenAPI code generation
- Production APIへの接続
- Cognitoの実JWT検証
- 本番相当の認証・認可Mock
- Statefulな業務ロジックの完全再現
- DBを持つ高機能Mock Backend
- 自動merge

---

## 完了後の位置づけ

```text
PBI
 ↓
SBI Planner
 ↓
API Schema Planner
 ↓
Human API Review / Approval
 ↓
Approved OpenAPI
 ├─ Mock Server → Expo / React Admin
 └─ Rails API implementation
 ↓
Contract / Acceptance Verification
```

API Schema Plannerで作った契約を実際の並行開発に使える状態までつなげることを目的とする。
title: 承認済みOpenAPIからローカルMock Serverを起動できるようにする

## Why

Lesson 9 imports a spec and then says "the demo API has no published spec, so write a small one". The gap it describes is the one `apic mock` (#152) fills: a spec is enough to have something to run the draft against. The lesson should show that step, because it is the moment the import loop closes.

## What changes

- Step 1's spec gains response content (a `Todo` schema with an example) so the mock has something to serve; the shown import output is regenerated from the real command.
- A new step between "Check the draft" and "Tidy the draft": start `apic mock todos-openapi.yaml --port 8090` in the background, run `list-todos` against it with `--var baseUrl=http://localhost:8090`, read the schema's example back, ask for the 404 with `Prefer: code=404`, then stop the mock. The point made in prose: the mock is the spec read back, so it proves the requests match the contract, and the demo is the stateful API the rest of the lesson needs.
- Later steps renumber; the episode script, `docs/learn/episodes/09.yaml`'s `blocks:` indices (the `TestSetupNamesRealBlocks` test guards them) and the syllabus row in `learn/index.md` follow.
- Every new block is marked `<!-- learn -->` and runs under `task learn:check`: the background server redirects its output to a file so the harness's pipe closes, and the last block kills it.

## Checklist

- [ ] lesson text, with outputs copied from a real run
- [ ] `learn/index.md` syllabus row and the lesson's `description:`
- [ ] `docs/learn/episodes/09.yaml` block indices and a talking point
- [ ] `task learn:check` green; Vale and codespell clean (`task docs:check`)
title: Lesson 9: run the imported draft against apic mock before the backend exists

body:
Explore whether Orval's mock generation could reduce the frontend test data and request handler code we maintain.

Orval already generates our API client, but mock generation is disabled in `frontend/orval.config.ts`. Playwright tests currently use handwritten JSON fixtures, payload helpers, and `page.route()` handlers.

Potential benefits:

- Generate response factories from OpenAPI instead of maintaining large JSON fixtures by hand.
- Keep test data aligned with API schema changes through regeneration, with small explicit overrides for scenario-specific values.
- Reuse generated MSW handlers across API-connected Storybook stories and component tests if those consumers need network mocking.

Evaluate a small pilot using generated factories in an existing Playwright test while keeping its current routing. Compare the maintained code and readability before and after. Assess MSW separately based on concrete reuse opportunities; migrating Playwright interception alone may offer little benefit.

The pilot should preserve deterministic IDs, dates, statuses, and relationships. Stateful mutations, authentication flows, and error scenarios will still need explicit behavior. Generated default responses do not replace those scenarios.

Record the maintenance savings, dependencies, limitations, and a recommendation before considering broader adoption.

References:

- https://orval.dev/docs/guides/faker/
- https://orval.dev/docs/guides/msw/
title: Explore Orval mock generation to reduce frontend test maintenance

body:
## Problem and feasibility
Move mobile HERE requests to MamaAir API so provider credentials, spending limits and failure handling are controlled on the server. Technically feasible with existing Django REST Framework, JWT, httpx and Redis support.

**Status: proposed implementation, production rollout gated on HERE use-case/licensing confirmation and verification of the current mobile source.** No live HERE request or account entitlement was tested.

### Evidence
- Mobile reference: [aq-geo-tracker-dev indoor_outdoor_classifier.dart](https://github.com/IAmJustAmateur/aq-geo-tracker-dev/blob/a3862041295f6b81b8c7409611b9f5384a3778e5/lib/logic/indoor_outdoor_classifier.dart), HEAD dated 2025-07-01; may not be the shipping app.
- Calls GET https://revgeocode.search.hereapi.com/v1/revgeocode with at, limit=1, lang=en-US and a hardcoded API key. Do not copy the credential into this issue or logs.
- Consumes id, distance, resultType, categories[].id, position. Heuristics/history/speed/GPS accuracy and local night hours determine indoor/outdoor.
- location_handler.dart configures location updates at approximately one minute; platform cadence is not guaranteed. Existing request suppression requires BOTH elapsed time <30s AND displacement <25m, so it is not a hard 30-second cap.
- Unknown is collapsed by isIndoor() into false; caller stores such points as outdoor. _lastPoiId is read but never updated in the inspected classifier. These are existing behavior concerns, not fixes achieved by moving HTTP.
- Backend has no HERE integration. api/urls.py, agent_api/settings.py, api/audit.py, docs/mobile_api_guide.md and docs/openapi/schema.json are integration points.
- Existing /api/movements/upload/json/ accepts optional boolean indoor; it cannot explicitly represent unknown. Do not silently reinterpret it during this migration.
- Related privacy/logging work: #35, #38, #40.

## Proposed first increment
One authenticated endpoint is sufficient for the observed call; do not add speculative address search/routing endpoints.

POST /api/location/reverse-geocode/
Authorization: Bearer <MamaAir access token>
Request:
```json
{"latitude":52.52,"longitude":13.405}
```

Backend fixes provider endpoint, limit=1 and lang=en-US to preserve existing behavior. Optional language support can be added only if the current app needs it. Validate finite latitude [-90,90], longitude [-180,180], body size and unknown fields. Never accept arbitrary upstream URLs, credentials, provider options or premium flags.

Proposed normalized success:
```json
{
  "provider":"here",
  "match":{
    "id":"<HERE result identifier>",
    "result_type":"houseNumber",
    "distance_m":12.3,
    "position":{"latitude":52.5201,"longitude":13.4051},
    "category_ids":[]
  }
}
```
Empty results: HTTP 200 with match:null. Nullable distance/position must be documented and handled; tolerate optional provider fields. Do not return full addresses or raw provider payload unnecessarily. This response is geographic context, NOT a verified indoor classification.

Keep stateful classification on mobile initially: adapt field mapping and replace the network call. Preserve exact GPS coordinates for this operation; coarse H3 rounding can materially change 35m/55m heuristic thresholds. Do not persist provider results by default.

### Failures, security and cost controls
- 400 invalid input; 401 unauthenticated/expired JWT; 429 our limit with Retry-After; 503 provider unavailable/quota/configuration unavailable; 504 provider timeout. Stable error.code and request_id; no provider URL/key or raw error text.
- Empty match must remain distinguishable from provider failure.
- Pooled HTTP client; explicit connect/read timeout and total request deadline (initial target <=5 seconds); no automatic provider retries in v1 to avoid amplification/billing.
- Server-only HERE_API_KEY, feature flag, safe disabled behavior, separate server App ID, separate environment credentials, documented rotation.
- Shared, atomic Redis rate/concurrency limits per user and globally, daily budget guard, fail closed for paid upstream calls if budget enforcement is unavailable. Configure from agreed entitlement; include other consumers of the same quota.
- Mobile: one request in flight, explicit minimum interval, backoff with jitter on 429/503, at most one JWT refresh/retry on 401; no direct-HERE fallback.
- Coordinate/body/response omission for this endpoint in AuditLog and application/proxy/APM logs, including validation errors. Suppress outgoing URL query strings containing apiKey and at. Safe metadata only.
- Metrics: operation counts, status, latency, estimated usage and alerts; no coordinates or user identifiers as metric labels.
- No cross-user/geospatial response cache or arbitrary TTL until HERE contract and response caching headers permit it. Redis counters are not a provider-result cache.

## Product limitations and release gates
1. HERE reverse geocoding returns nearby address/POI/street or area, not building containment or reliable indoor/outdoor. Validate classifier separately against labeled real-world data.
2. HERE's published Limited/Base exclusions include Asset Management and define an asset to include a person/application user. Continuous tracking with exposure analytics may fall within this definition. Obtain written confirmation of plan/use case, background calls, derivative classifications, retention and attribution before production activation; do not assume buying Base Plan resolves this.
3. Limited Plan without payment information is currently listed as 1,000 requests/day and 5 RPS for Geocode & Reverse Geocode. A theoretical continuous one-request/minute user generates 1,440/day; 100 users at 8h/day generate 48,000/day (~1.44m/30 days), excluding retries. These are sizing examples, not observed billing.
4. Confirm actual free allowance, paid rates, RPS, attribution and retention in the account/contract; no dollar quote is established here.
5. On network failure preserve measurement data and distinguish unknown from confirmed outdoor. Before rollout agree whether to preserve legacy fallback temporarily or introduce versioned tri-state storage/upload; never silently change exposure semantics.
6. Inventory all HERE calls in the current shipping mobile app before declaring migration complete.

## Implementation checklist / acceptance criteria
- [ ] Confirm current mobile repository/revision and enumerate HERE calls.
- [ ] Record HERE use-case approval and plan, retention/attribution requirements; provision server app credentials.
- [ ] Implement provider adapter, validated serializers and JWT-protected endpoint; no migrations expected for stateless reverse geocoding alone.
- [ ] Add distributed rate/budget controls, timeouts, safe logging and monitoring.
- [ ] Tests with mocked HERE: normal/empty/partial/malformed responses, timeout, 429/5xx, invalid/missing config, auth, nonfinite/out-of-range coordinates, no sensitive data in logs, concurrent quota enforcement and quota-store failure. Default tests never consume paid HERE.
- [ ] Publish OpenAPI snapshot, mobile guide, examples and error contract.
- [ ] Update actual mobile caller, token handling, bounded retries and network-failure policy; test on device with existing classifier.
- [ ] Staging end-to-end with a server key after entitlement confirmation; verify actual HERE response fields and latency.
- [ ] Roll out backend then mobile behind a feature flag; observe usage and errors.
- [ ] Remove embedded key from mobile source/build configuration, assess prior exposure and rotate/revoke the old key with an explicit old-client cutoff. Rollback must not restore server secrets to mobile.

## Owner setup guide
1. Identify who owns the existing HERE account/key; reuse the organization if appropriate. A new account is only necessary if none is controlled by the project.
2. Ask HERE to confirm: background reverse geocoding of consenting users' GPS roughly once/minute, indoor/outdoor heuristics and personal air-exposure analytics; expected countries/users/hours; server-mediated access; retained derived data. Request a plan/quote and allowed caching/attribution.
3. In platform.here.com register a separate backend application in Access Manager > Apps; enable/subscribe the agreed Geocoding & Search service.
4. Generate an API key under Credentials > API Keys; place it only in deployment secrets as HERE_API_KEY after implementation. Do not paste it into GitHub or chat.
5. Agree daily/monthly budget and peak rate, then staging validation and gradual mobile rollout.
6. Coordinate revocation of the existing mobile key; old builds that still call HERE will lose this feature after revocation.

## Official references (checked 2026-10-15)
- [Reverse geocode semantics](https://docs.here.com/geocoding-and-search/docs/reverse-geocode)
- [Reverse geocode API](https://docs.here.com/geocoding-and-search/reference/get_revgeocode)
- [RPS limits, excluded use cases and App IDs](https://www.here.com/get-started/pricing/rps-limits-excluded-use-cases)
- [API keys and rotation](https://docs.here.com/identity-and-access-management/docs/plat-using-apikeys)
- [Platform terms and caching restrictions](https://legal.here.com/us-en/terms/here-platform-terms)
- [Pricing: confirm in account/quote](https://www.here.com/get-started/pricing)
title: Move mobile HERE reverse geocoding behind authenticated backend API; confirm tracking entitlement before rollout
