## Visión validada por el propietario
ProtocolIA debe ser una fábrica personal de software: requisitos en lenguaje natural → contratos revisables/editables → aplicación real dentro de perfiles soportados → pruebas y documentación que permitan entenderla años después. La interacción humana es opcional para decisiones técnicas reversibles, nunca una autorización automática para operaciones sensibles.

## Punto de partida
- PR experimental R1: https://github.com/barbasmarcosi/ProtocolIA/pull/105
- ADR y protocolo: `docs/research/autonomous-engineering/` (rama R1).
- **No existe todavía ninguna ejecución comparativa de herramientas candidatas**: las CI de R1 son únicamente del gate local/fixtures sintéticos.

## R2 — Evaluación y contratos autónomos (sin reinventar el compilador)
- Congelar holdouts no publicados, oráculos y presupuesto comparable por herramienta.
- Ejecutar A directo, B generadores comunes, C1 Superpowers+OPSX, C2 Spec Kit+TypeSpec, C3 GSD Core+OPSX+TypeSpec; BMAD critic ablation opcional.
- Medir decisiones inventadas, tiempo y intervención, contratos válidos, completitud y código funcional.
- Formalizar el formato de `requirements/decisions` → TypeSpec y referencia de proveniencia. Implementar `autonomous_reviewable` y `review_contracts` sin tocar permisos externos.
- Cerrar solo con pruebas independientes, resultados negativos incluidos y selección razonada.

## R3 — Project Passport (documentación como entregable)
- Desde el IR + fuentes explícitas: glosario, mapa requerimiento→contrato→API/DB/UI→test, diagramas textuales C4/ER/estados y ADR con procedencia.
- Aplicación generada ejecutable sin ProtocolIA en runtime; docs legibles sin IA.
- Tests de generación determinista, hashes, detección de drift, omisión segura de racionales desconocidos y exportación estática.

## R4 — Two-Year Handoff Test
- Proyecto desconocido al agente, sin acceso a los chats originales.
- Localizar y explicar reglas y decisiones, construir/reproducir el sistema, evolucionar una funcionalidad, conservar datos y actualizar documentación.
- Probar en disposable PostgreSQL/HTTP/Chromium con regresiones; fallar explícitamente ante incertidumbre de políticas comerciales.
- Documentar límites y costo total frente a agente directo.

## No objetivos / límites
No nuevos tags, deployments de producción, banca real, cambio en TL-14 #57 ni fusión automática de R1. No adoptar frameworks de agentes sin comparar versiones actuales, dependencias y licencias. Un análisis documental no es una validación experimental.

**Condición de cierre:** evidencia real sobre los gates, no textos ni número de commits.
title: R2–R4: evaluar workflows autónomos y entregar Project Passport + prueba de retoma

body:
Go recordings and implementation details still decide many Rust test expectations. Replace those expectations with tests of supported client, operator, and provider behavior.

This tracks the remaining test migration after #45 retired Go differential and benchmark gates.

## Go parity test inventory — 2026-11-14

Source audit at `f6bff59c4c1646747caced0fbb08388fd66626e0` found **552 Rust test entry points** associated with Go expectations or requiring classification:

| Disposition | Tests | Action |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Go-only expectations | 70 | Remove or narrow Go-specific assertions; retain any useful behavioral subset. |
| Useful coverage with Go as authority | 444 | Replace recorded expectations with independently specified Rust tests. |
| Independently justified coverage | 38 | Keep behavior, security, and first-party regressions. |

The inventory also lists **46 historical Go recorder tests** and **16 historical Python audit tests**, separately from Rust tests. Each entry describes its value, an idiomatic Rust replacement approach, and replacement difficulty on a **1–5 scale**. These counts are test entry points, not individual fixture cases; mixed-purpose tests are not blanket deletion candidates.

### Full inventory

[Part 1](https://github.com/zakstak/cliproxy-rs/issues/198#issuecomment-6884169128) · [Part 2](https://github.com/zakstak/cliproxy-rs/issues/198#issuecomment-6884169375) · [Part 3](https://github.com/zakstak/cliproxy-rs/issues/198#issuecomment-6884169636) · [Part 4](https://github.com/zakstak/cliproxy-rs/issues/198#issuecomment-6884169828) · [Part 5](https://github.com/zakstak/cliproxy-rs/issues/198#issuecomment-6884170076) · [Part 6](https://github.com/zakstak/cliproxy-rs/issues/198#issuecomment-6884170262)

All source links in the inventory are pinned to the audited revision. The complete report is reproduced in the linked comments, including each test, its value, its Rust replacement approach, and its difficulty rating.

### Suggested migration order

1. Remove recorder bookkeeping as its replay is replaced, then exact Go error prose, header casing, JSON layout, and display formatting assertions. Preserve validation, redaction, precision, and byte preservation.
2. Replace helper goldens with explicit boundary tables and properties. Retain operator-used configuration spellings, saved credential compatibility, and shared Home keys where required.
3. Split broad translator and executor replays into endpoint and protocol tests using local mocks and private auth directories. Preserve streaming, auth, retry, usage, persistence, and multi-turn coverage. Complete one provider or route before removing its replay.
4. Remove the unused Go recording toolchain and regeneration instructions after active dependencies are gone.

Provider documentation, first-party clients, and verified wire behavior should define expectations. Codex replacements must follow `docs/codex/CONTRACT.md`; unresolved behavior remains unknown. No replacement requires running Go.

This is a source audit and migration inventory. No runtime tests, provider requests, production changes, or deployments were performed.

## Completion criteria

- [ ] Review the 70 Go-only expectations and remove or narrow them while retaining useful assertions.
- [ ] Replace Go as the authority for the 444 migration tests with independently justified expectations.
- [ ] Retain the 38 independently justified tests.
- [ ] Remove unused Go recorders and regeneration instructions once no active test depends on them.
- [ ] Preserve supported clients, operator configuration, credential files, security, streaming, and raw-byte passthrough.
title: Replace Go parity test expectations with idiomatic Rust behavior tests

body:
> Part of #1's R2, in three specs: **E** #133 HTTP/2 (h2c and TLS); **F** #134 gRPC unary, on top of E; **G** #135 LLM API presets, in parallel with E. Decided with the maintainer on 2026-10-23. The text below calls them spec E, F and G. It continues in the first comment.

## Problem Statement

Many of the services that smock's users test call their dependencies over gRPC. smock cannot stand in for those dependencies:

- **Messages are binary, and the status is in trailers.** Spec E brings HTTP/2, but a gRPC call carries a protobuf message in a 5-byte frame and ends with its status in HTTP/2 trailers. A Stub can match the message only as bytes, cannot answer with a message built from JSON, and cannot send trailers. A gRPC client reads every answer smock can give as an error.
- **A second tool.** Teams run GripMock, the WireMock gRPC extension or MockServer beside smock. Each has its own format, its own port or process and its own journal, and none has smock's Sessions, Scenarios, Variables or Data buckets. A test with one HTTP and one gRPC dependency keeps two mocks in step.
- **Errors cannot be written.** Clients branch on the gRPC status (NOT_FOUND, UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED), on trailing metadata, and on error details such as RetryInfo or BadRequest.
- **Misses are opaque.** A call that nothing matches gets an HTTP 404 with a JSON body. The client reports UNIMPLEMENTED with a message about an unexpected content type, and the test author never learns which Stub came closest.
- **Tools expect the usual services.** grpcurl and Postman find a server's methods through server reflection. Clients and proxies that health-check a dependency call the standard health service.
- **Deadlines and failures.** Testing a client's deadlines and retries needs a dependency that is slow, that fails one call in ten, or that drops a stream. smock has delays and Faults, but nothing maps them onto gRPC.

## Solution

smock serves gRPC unary calls on its plain (h2c) and TLS (h2) ports, beside HTTP, on top of spec E.

- **Recognised by content type.** An HTTP/2 request whose content type is `application/grpc`, alone or followed by `+` or `;`, is a gRPC call. Everything else goes to the HTTP Stubs, as today.
- **Descriptor sets.** A Mock names a Descriptor set ("set" for short in this spec): a self-contained FileDescriptorSet, built with `buf build` or `protoc --include_imports`, in the body-file subdirectory. It loads with the Definition files: reloads, the digest, symlink containment and `smock check` apply. smock parses no `.proto` file and ships no protoc.
- **Ordinary Stubs.** A Stub whose exact `path` names a method of its Mock's set, such as `/helloworld.Greeter/SayHello`, is a gRPC Stub. Its `json` body condition and its `json` reply are checked against the method's types when the files load.
- **One engine.** smock decodes the request message to JSON and hands the engine an ordinary request: POST, the method's path, the metadata as headers, the JSON as the body. Conditions, templates, Sessions, Scenarios, Variables, Data buckets, the Near miss and the Journal work unchanged. smock encodes the reply JSON with the output type.
- **gRPC replies.** `response.grpc` gives the status by name, a message, trailing metadata and error details. `headers` are the initial metadata.
- **Misses.** An unmatched call gets UNIMPLEMENTED, with the Near miss in a `smock-near-miss` trailer.
- **Deadlines, Faults and built-in services.** A delay that outlasts `grpc-timeout` ends in DEADLINE_EXCEEDED. Faults take spec E's per-stream forms. Server reflection and health can be turned on per Mock.
- **smock's own code.** The protobuf codec and the gRPC wire rules are two new I/O-free protocol modules of smock. No new dependency, no C.

```yaml
mocks:
  - name: greeter
    hosts: [greeter.svc]
    grpc:
      descriptorSet: greeter.binpb   # in the body-file subdirectory, like a bodyFile
      reflection: true               # off unless turned on
      health: true                   # off unless turned on
stubs:
  - id: hello-tom
    mock: greeter
    request:
      path: /helloworld.Greeter/SayHello      # names a unary method of the set
      headers: { x-tenant: acme }             # metadata, as headers
      body: { json: { name: Tom } }           # the message as ProtoJSON
    response:
      headers: { x-served-by: smock }         # initial metadata
      json: { message: Hello Tom }            # encoded with the output type
  - id: hello-unknown
    mock: greeter
    request:
      path: /helloworld.Greeter/SayHello
    response:
      template: true
      grpc:
        status: NOT_FOUND
        message: no user called ${body.name}
        trailers: { x-trace: abc }
        details:
          - "@type": type.googleapis.com/google.rpc.ErrorInfo   # a type of the set
            reason: USER_UNKNOWN
            domain: greeter.svc
```

`grpcurl -plaintext -authority greeter.svc -H 'x-tenant: acme' -d '{"name":"Tom"}' localhost:8080 helloworld.Greeter/SayHello` gets `{"message": "Hello Tom"}`, the set found through reflection. With `"Ann"`, it gets `NOT_FOUND` and the message `no user called Ann`. The Journal records both calls with the decoded JSON body and their gRPC status.

## User Stories

### Clients and ports

1. As a test author whose service calls a gRPC dependency, I want smock to answer its unary calls, so that one mock serves my HTTP and gRPC dependencies.
2. As a test author, I want gRPC on the plain port over h2c and on the TLS port over h2, so that I need no new port, Service or address.
3. As a test author, I want a gRPC call recognised by its content type, so that HTTP Stubs on the same port keep answering everything else.
4. As a test author, I want `application/grpc+proto` and `application/grpc` with parameters accepted, as gRPC libraries accept them, so that every client's content type works.
5. As a test author, I want a content type such as `application/grpc+json` refused with a gRPC error, so that my client says plainly that smock does not speak it.
6. As a test author, I want a gRPC content type sent over HTTP/1.1 treated as an ordinary HTTP request, so that the HTTP/1.1 path is unchanged.
7. As a platform engineer, I want the docs to say that `--tls-http2 off` also turns off gRPC over TLS, so that I know what the flag costs.
8. As a test author, I want grpcurl to work with `-plaintext` on the plain port and over TLS on the TLS port, so that I can try calls by hand.
9. As a test author, I want `:authority` to choose the Mock, so that grpcurl's `-authority` or my channel's target picks the Mock, and the Default Mock answers other Hosts.

### Descriptor sets

10. As a test author, I want to give smock a Descriptor set built with `buf build` or `protoc --include_imports`, so that I reuse the build my project already has.
11. As a platform engineer, I want smock to parse no `.proto` file and ship no protoc, so that the image stays one binary.
12. As a test author, I want a set with a missing dependency to be a load error that names the missing file, so that a forgotten `--include_imports` shows before a test runs.
13. As a test author, I want to keep the set in the body-file subdirectory and point at it from the Mock, as I point at body files, so that it lives in version control beside my Stubs.
14. As a platform engineer, I want a changed set reloaded with the Definition files, in one swap, so that no call is decoded with one version and answered with another.
15. As a platform engineer, I want the set to count in the definition set digest, so that replicas that serve the same schema report the same digest.
16. As a security reviewer, I want the set's path held inside the body-file subdirectory, symlinks included, so that a Definition file cannot read a file outside it.
17. As a test author, I want each Mock to name its own set, so that two Mocks can impersonate two versions of one service.
18. As a test author, I want `smock check` to read the sets and check every gRPC Stub against them, so that CI catches a schema change that breaks my Stubs.
19. As a test author, I want proto3 and proto2 types served, with closed enums, required fields, extensions and groups, so that older services can be mocked too.
20. As a test author, I want a Stub on a method whose types come from an editions file to be a load error that says editions come in a later spec, so that I am never served a wrong encoding.
21. As a test author, I want editions files that no Stub uses to load quietly, so that a large shared set stays usable.
22. As a test author, I want source info and custom options in a set to cost nothing, so that a set built with `buf build`'s defaults works as it is.
23. As a test author, I want the well-known types (Timestamp, Duration, Struct, the wrappers, FieldMask, Empty, Any) in their ProtoJSON forms, so that my JSON reads as grpcurl prints it.

### gRPC Stubs

24. As a test author, I want to write a gRPC Stub as an ordinary Stub, with `path: /pkg.Service/Method`, so that I learn nothing new to start.
25. As a test author, I want to leave out `method`, since a gRPC call is always a POST, so that my Stubs stay short.
26. As a test author, I want `json` body conditions on the request message, with patterns and operators, so that I match on fields as for a JSON API.
27. As a test author, I want a Stub's conditions checked against the input type when the files load, so that a misspelt field or a value of the wrong type is an error, not a Stub that never matches.
28. As a test author, I want a condition value that ProtoJSON reads but never prints, such as a Duration of `"1.5s"`, to be a load error that names the printed form (`"1.500s"`), so that I learn of it at load, not from a Stub that never matches.
29. As a test author, I want to write field names as the `.proto` spells them or in lowerCamelCase, and enums by name or by number, so that I can copy from the schema or from grpcurl.
30. As a test author, I want gRPC Stubs to answer only gRPC calls, and gRPC calls to be answered only by gRPC Stubs, so that a catch-all HTTP Stub never turns a call into an error.
31. As a test author, I want fields that make no sense for gRPC refused at load (query, cookie, form and xml conditions, text bodies, an HTTP status, body files, events), so that I learn at once what a gRPC Stub can do.
32. As a test author, I want priority, Scenarios, Variables, data writes, weighted `responses` and Faults on gRPC Stubs, so that stateful and flaky dependencies work as over HTTP.
33. As a test author, I want to add gRPC Stubs as Ephemeral Stubs through the Admin API, checked like file Stubs, so that a test can arrange its own answers.
34. As a test author, I want `smock check` to warn about a Stub whose path looks like a gRPC method but names none in its Mock's set, so that a typo does not leave an HTTP Stub that gRPC calls never reach.

### The JSON form

35. As a test author, I want the request message as ProtoJSON with lowerCamelCase names, so that conditions read like grpcurl's output.
36. As a test author, I want 64-bit integers as JSON numbers, so that `{"id": 123}` matches and integers compare exactly at any size.
37. As a test author, I want fields without presence printed even at their default, so that `{"count": 0}` or `{"name": ""}` can match.
38. As a test author, I want empty repeated and map fields printed as `[]` and `{}`, so that I can match "no items".
39. As a test author, I want fields with presence (proto3 `optional`, proto2 fields, messages, oneof members) printed only when set, so that `$exists` tells set from unset.
40. As a test author, I want enums printed by name, so that conditions say `ACTIVE`, not `1`.
41. As a test author, I want an unknown value of an open enum printed as its number, so that a newer client's value still shows.
42. As a test author, I want `float` fields printed as protobuf's JSON printers print them, so that `{"price": 9.99}` matches a float field holding 9.99.
43. As a test author, I want unknown fields in a request skipped, so that a newer client still matches my Stubs.
44. As a test author, I want the same message always to give the same JSON text, so that `bodyText`, the Journal and the Near miss read the same whatever client sent it.
45. As a test author, I want templates, `find`, Variables and data writes to see the lowerCamelCase names only, so that there is one spelling at run time.
46. As a test author, I want reply JSON read as ProtoJSON, with either name spelling, enum names or numbers, and 64-bit integers as numbers or strings, so that I can paste a reply from any tool.

### Metadata

47. As a test author, I want request metadata shown as headers and matched by `headers` conditions, so that I match on `authorization` or `x-tenant` as over HTTP.
48. As a test author, I want no field hidden, `content-type`, `grpc-timeout` and `user-agent` included, so that I can match on them too.
49. As a test author, I want `-bin` metadata shown without base64 padding, and the padding removed from my exact conditions on it, so that padded and unpadded clients match alike.
50. As a test author, I want the Session read from `baggage` metadata, as from the HTTP header, so that tests sharing one channel stay apart.
51. As a test author, I want `header.NAME` in templates to read metadata, so that a reply can echo a request ID.

### Replies

52. As a test author, I want the reply message written as `json` and encoded with the method's output type, so that I write replies as I write JSON responses.
53. As a test author, I want a static reply that does not fit the output type to be a load error, so that `smock check` catches it.
54. As a test author, I want templated replies rendered as JSON and then encoded, so that I can build a message from the request.
55. As a test author, I want a templated reply that does not fit the output type to give INTERNAL, with the reason in the Journal, so that I can see what went wrong.
56. As a test author, I want a Stub without `json` to answer an empty message, so that methods returning `Empty` need no body.
57. As a test author, I want `headers` sent as initial metadata, so that clients that read response headers can be tested.
58. As a test author, I want to set trailing metadata, so that clients that read trailers can be tested.
59. As a test author, I want several values of one name as an array, and `-bin` values in base64, so that I can write any metadata.
60. As a test author, I want reserved names (`grpc-*`, `content-type`, `te`) refused in my metadata at load, so that I cannot break the protocol by accident.
61. As a test author, I want smock to set the reply's content type, so that clients always read the reply as gRPC.

### Status, message and details

62. As a test author, I want to give the gRPC status by name, such as `NOT_FOUND`, so that Stubs read like my client's code.
63. As a test author, I want the status to default to OK, so that a success Stub needs no `grpc` field.
64. As a test author, I want to write the status message in any Unicode text, percent-encoded by smock, so that spaces, accents and emoji arrive exactly.
65. As a test author, I want the message templated with `template: true`, so that it can name the requested resource.
66. As a test author, I want error details such as `ErrorInfo`, `RetryInfo` or `BadRequest` written in ProtoJSON with `@type`, so that I can test clients that use gRPC's richer error model.
67. As a test author, I want detail types looked up in my Mock's set, and a missing type to be a load error, so that no detail silently goes out empty.
68. As a test author, I want smock to build `google.rpc.Status` from the status and message I gave, so that the details never contradict the status.
69. As a test author, I want an error Stub that also gives a message body to be a load error, so that I do not wonder why my client never sees it.
70. As a test author, I want a gRPC Stub unable to set an HTTP status, so that every reply from a Stub is valid gRPC.
71. As a test author, I want an error reply without initial metadata sent as Trailers-Only, as gRPC servers send it, so that my client sees what a real server sends.
72. As a test author, I want weighted `responses` that mix OK and error statuses, so that a dependency can fail one call in ten.
73. As a test author, I want a data write that cannot be applied, or writes past the state bound, answered with a gRPC status, so that my client never gets an HTTP 500 or 507.
74. As a test author, I want a reply whose metadata is too large for my client replaced by INTERNAL with a plain message, so that my client never reports a framing error instead of the status.

### Unmatched calls

75. As a test author, I want an unmatched call to get UNIMPLEMENTED with a fixed message, so that my client sees the code it expects for a missing method, and tests that check messages stay stable.
76. As a test author, I want the Near miss in a `smock-near-miss` trailer, in the form of the HTTP header, so that I see the closest Stub in my client's log.
77. As a test author, I want unmatched calls in the Journal with their full Near miss, and in the unmatched list, so that a test can report what it missed.
78. As a test author, I want a call to a method the Mock's set lacks, or to a Mock without a set, answered UNIMPLEMENTED at once, so that my client does not wait for a timeout.
79. As a test author, I want a call to a streaming method answered UNIMPLEMENTED at once, and a Stub on one refused at load with a pointer to R3, so that I know streaming is not served yet.
80. As a test author, I want a call for a Host no Mock answers to get UNIMPLEMENTED in gRPC form, so that my client does not report a content-type error.

### Protocol rules and limits

81. As a test author, I want my client's compressed messages refused with UNIMPLEMENTED and `grpc-accept-encoding: identity`, so that the client knows to send them uncompressed.
82. As a test author, I want an uncompressed message served even when my client announces `grpc-encoding: gzip`, so that clients that only offer compression work.
83. As a security reviewer, I want smock never to decompress, so that a compression bomb cannot exhaust memory.
84. As a test author, I want replies never compressed, so that any client can read them.
85. As a test author, I want a call with no message or with several messages refused with UNIMPLEMENTED, as gRPC libraries refuse it.
86. As a test author, I want a message of zero octets served as a message with every field at its default, so that a call taking `Empty` works.
87. As a test author, I want a message over the body limit refused with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, so that the limit reads as gRPC's own.
88. As a test author, I want a non-POST call answered 405 with INTERNAL, and a malformed `grpc-timeout` 400 with INTERNAL, as grpc-go answers them.
89. As a test author, I want a call without `te: trailers` accepted, so that every real client works, strict or not.
90. As a test author, I want a message that does not parse refused with INTERNAL, as gRPC libraries refuse it.
91. As a security reviewer, I want the decoder bounded in nesting depth, in lengths and in the size of the JSON it prints, so that a small hostile message cannot exhaust CPU or memory.

### Deadlines

92. As a test author, I want a delay that outlasts the client's `grpc-timeout` to end in DEADLINE_EXCEEDED at the deadline, so that even a client that does not enforce deadlines sees what a real server sends.
93. As a test author, I want such a call recorded in the Journal with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, even when my client resets the stream at its own deadline first, so that I can assert the timeout happened.
94. As a load-test engineer, I want a call past its deadline to free its stream at once, so that slow Stubs do not pile up work.

### Faults

95. As a test author, I want a `reset` Fault to reset only the call's stream, so that my client sees INTERNAL while other calls on the channel succeed.
96. As a test author, I want a `partial` Fault to send the reply's headers and half the framed message, then reset the stream, so that I can test a truncated reply.
97. As a test author, I want a `close` Fault to send GOAWAY and close the connection, and the docs to warn that it ends every call on it, so that I test a lost connection knowingly.
98. As a test author, I want the docs to say which gRPC status each Fault gives a client, so that I can write my assertions.
99. As a test author, I want probabilistic gRPC errors written as weighted responses, so that no new Fault kind is needed.

### State and the rest of smock

100. As a test author, I want Scenarios to move on gRPC calls, so that a "create, then get" flow works.
101. As a test author, I want gRPC Stubs to read and write Variables and Data buckets, so that an item created over gRPC or HTTP can be fetched by a later call over either.
102. As a test author, I want the Default Mock to answer gRPC calls with its own set, so that one Mock can serve a service whose Host I do not know in advance.
103. As a test author, I want a call my client cancels during a delay to end there, as any HTTP/2 stream does, so that smock does no more work for it.

### The Journal and the Admin API

104. As a test author, I want a gRPC call's Journal entry to show the request message as decoded JSON, so that I can read what my client sent.
105. As a test author, I want the entry to carry the gRPC status by name, so that I can assert which status a call got.
106. As a test author, I want Journal queries and verification to filter gRPC calls by Mock, path and metadata, as for HTTP, so that call counts need no new syntax.
107. As a client developer, I want the Admin API's OpenAPI document to describe the new field, so that my generated client accepts it.
108. As a test author, I want `smock render` and the Admin render to render a gRPC Stub from a sample message and show the reply JSON, status and trailers, so that I can check a templated reply without a client.

### Built-in services

109. As a test author, I want to turn server reflection on for a Mock, so that grpcurl and Postman can list and describe its services without a local copy of the set.
110. As a security reviewer, I want reflection off unless a Mock turns it on, so that a schema is shown only where its owner asked.
111. As a test author, I want reflection v1 and v1alpha answered, so that older and newer tools work.
112. As a test author, I want reflection to send files without source info, dependencies included, so that answers stay small and complete.
113. As a test author, I want to turn the standard health service on for a Mock, so that clients and proxies that health-check their dependency find it healthy.
114. As a test author, I want health to say SERVING for the empty name and for each service in the set, and NOT_FOUND for others, as gRPC's health servers do.
115. As an operator, I want health to say NOT_SERVING once SIGTERM starts the drain, so that health-checking clients move away before smock stops.
116. As a test author, I want my own Stub on a health method to win over the built-in answer, so that a Scenario can make the service NOT_SERVING.
117. As an operator, I want health and reflection calls left out of the Journal but counted in the metrics, so that frequent checks do not evict the calls my tests verify.

### Operations

118. As an operator, I want client keepalive PINGs answered under spec E's limits, with no separate gRPC rule, so that one set of defences covers both.
119. As an operator, I want SIGTERM to send GOAWAY and let calls in flight finish, so that clients start new calls elsewhere.
120. As an operator, I want the docs to say that an idle channel gets GOAWAY after the idle timeout, so that I understand reconnects in client logs.
121. As an operator, I want the request metrics to count gRPC calls with the same labels, and refused calls as rejected traffic, so that dashboards need no change.
122. As a platform engineer, I want the memory targets (idle RSS 20 MiB, peak 32 MiB) to hold with gRPC, so that small Pods still fit.

### Code and supply chain

123. As a contributor, I want the protobuf codec and the gRPC wire rules to be I/O-free protocol modules of smock, so that the no-I/O rule holds and they can be published on mooncakes later.
124. As a security reviewer, I want no new dependency and no C for gRPC, so that the supply chain does not grow.
125. As a maintainer, I want those modules tested through their public interfaces, adversarial inputs included, as #1 requires of protocol modules.

### Tests, benchmarks and docs

126. As a maintainer, I want e2e tests that make gRPC calls over real sockets, so that the mapping is tested from outside.
127. As a maintainer, I want grpcurl, at a pinned version, to call smock in CI, so that a real client checks every change.
128. As a maintainer, I want protobuf's conformance suite run against the codec, binary and JSON, with a committed failure list, so that ProtoJSON's edge cases are covered and regressions show.
129. As a maintainer, I want the descriptor fixtures rebuilt from their `.proto` sources in CI and compared, so that the committed binaries cannot drift.
130. As a load-test engineer, I want a gRPC case in the benchmark, locally and on GKE, so that the codec's cost is measured where smock runs.
131. As a maintainer, I want the e2e benchmark test to check each gRPC call's status, since oha sees only `:status`, so that a run of errors cannot pass as success.
132. As a test author, I want a guide page on gRPC with a table from protobuf types to JSON, so that I can write Stubs without reading the protobuf docs.
133. As a maintainer, I want gRPC shipped after spec E, so that it builds on a tested HTTP/2.

## Implementation Decisions

The rules below are the maintainer's decisions of 2026-10-23, listed in Further Notes, or follow from them, from spec E, from #1 and from the ADRs.

### Ports and detection

- **The same ports as HTTP.** gRPC is served on the plain port (h2c by prior knowledge) and the TLS port (ALPN `h2`), beside HTTP, with no port of its own. With `--tls-http2 off`, gRPC over TLS is unavailable. The admin port never serves gRPC.
- **By content type.** On an HTTP/2 stream, a `content-type` that is `application/grpc`, or that starts with `application/grpc+` or `application/grpc;`, makes the request a gRPC call. Any other content type, or none, goes to the HTTP Stubs as today.
  - The subtype is the text after `+`, up to any `;`. No subtype, or `proto`, is served.
  - Any other subtype, such as `json`, is refused with UNIMPLEMENTED and `:status` 200. `+json` can be added later without changing this routing.
- **HTTP/1.1.** A gRPC content type over HTTP/1.1 makes an ordinary HTTP request (HTTP Stubs, then `noMatch`). gRPC needs HTTP/2 trailers.
- **Spec E's checks come first.** A stream that spec E answers 400 (a malformed request) or 431 (too many or too large header fields) keeps that answer, with no gRPC status. A gRPC client reads them as INTERNAL and UNKNOWN, through gRPC's table for answers that are not gRPC.

### Descriptor sets

- **The Mock field.** A Mock gains `grpc`, a closed object:
  - `descriptorSet`: the path of a set in the body-file subdirectory, with the rules of `bodyFile`: it stays inside, symlinks included, and none of its names starts with `.`.
  - `reflection` and `health`: booleans, `false` by default.
  - `descriptorSet` may be left out when a Mock wants only the built-in services.
- **Self-contained sets only.** A set is a FileDescriptorSet in protobuf's binary encoding, as `protoc --include_imports -o` and `buf build -o` write it. Every dependency of every file must be in the set. A missing one is a load error that names the file and its missing import. smock parses no `.proto` text and runs no protoc.
- **Read with the Definition files.** A set is read in the same load and swapped in with the same definition set, so a call is never decoded with one version and answered with another. It counts in the digest as a body file does, and the watch covers it. A problem is reported with the Definition file and the JSON Pointer of `descriptorSet`, by `smock check`, at startup and by a reload, which then keeps the set it serves.
- **Checks at load.** The set decodes; each file appears once; each full name is defined once; every type that a field, a method or an extension names resolves within the set. Unknown fields of the set, such as Buf's image extensions, are skipped.
- **Per Mock.** Each Mock has its own set, so two Mocks may hold two versions of one package. The Default Mock and Ephemeral Stubs use their Mock's set.
- **What is kept.** SourceCodeInfo is dropped at load: nothing reads comments, and it makes sets far larger. Options other than `map_entry`, `packed` and `message_set_wire_format` (below) are ignored.
- **Syntax.** proto3 and proto2 are served, proto2's closed enums, required fields, extensions and groups included.
  - A Stub whose method's input or output type, or any type reached from them, is defined in an editions file is a load error that says editions come in a later spec. So is a detail type from such a file. The check is per method: editions files that no Stub uses load quietly.
  - A request message without a proto2 required field is refused with INTERNAL, as protobuf's parsers refuse it, and a reply without one is a load error, or INTERNAL when templated.
  - Unknown values of a closed enum are kept as unknown fields, as protobuf keeps them, so matching skips them. Extensions show in JSON under `[full.name]` keys, as ProtoJSON writes them.
  - A Stub whose types, or detail types, reach a message with `message_set_wire_format` is a load error, per method, as for editions: MessageSet extensions use another wire form, which smock does not encode (FX2).

### Where the code lives

- **Two protocol modules of smock.** `smock/protobuf`: the wire codec, descriptor reading, messages decoded and encoded from descriptors, and ProtoJSON. `smock/grpc`: message framing, status codes and their names, the metadata rules, `grpc-message` percent-encoding, `grpc-timeout` and the content type.
  - Neither imports the other, nor any other module. Both build for wasm-gc. The no-I/O check's rules are unchanged: the two modules join both of its lists, the protocol modules and the imports its no-I/O packages may use, as the check expects of a new protocol module. The no-I/O packages may import them, as they import the HTTP/1.1 codec. They are published on mooncakes once their interfaces settle, as #1 plans.
- **No new dependency.** No moonbitlang/protobuf, moonrpc or moonproto: none decodes messages from descriptors, and the no-I/O rule would need changing. ADR 0001 holds as written: gRPC framing is smock's to build. No new ADR.
- **Who uses them.** The definitions package reads sets and checks Stubs at load. The server package's gRPC layer decodes, maps and encodes. The engine reads status names. The engine never decodes protobuf.
- **Two printing forms.** The protobuf module prints canonical ProtoJSON, and smock's decoded form (below). smock serves calls with its decoded form; the conformance testee uses canonical ProtoJSON.

### From a call to the engine

- **The gRPC layer.** It lives in the server package, beside spec E's HTTP/2 mapping. It takes a stream whose HEADERS carry a gRPC content type, checks them, collects the message, decodes it, calls the engine, encodes the reply and writes it.
- **Two lookups.** When the HEADERS arrive, the gRPC layer asks the engine for the call's Mock, the Default Mock included, and that Mock's set, from the snapshot the engine serves. This decides only the answers given from the HEADERS (below). When the request ends, the layer looks them up again from the current snapshot, then decodes, calls `handle` and encodes the reply with no await between them, so a reload cannot split them. A call that now fails a HEADERS-time check (no Mock, no set, the method gone or no longer unary) gets that check's UNIMPLEMENTED answer and message. Today's Host lookup answers nothing even when there is a Default Mock, so this is a new call.
- **The request the engine sees.**
  - The method is `POST`; the target is `:path`; the version is `HTTP/2`; the Host comes from `:authority`, through spec E's authority input.
  - The headers are the metadata as received, every field, none hidden. `-bin` values lose their base64 padding in each comma-separated element, commas kept, since a proxy may join repeated fields with commas. smock never decodes them.
  - The body is the decoded message, as JSON text in smock's decoded form (below).
- **The gRPC call marker.** `handle` gains one optional input that marks the request as a gRPC call, names its method, and carries the count of octets the stream's DATA frames brought, which the entry records as its body size. The request's shape is unchanged; HTTP never gives the input, so existing calls and Seam 1 tests stay as they are.
- **The final gRPC status.** A Journal entry gains a method that the server calls before it commits the entry, beside `finish`, which runs after. It sets the gRPC status the call really got: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED at the deadline, or INTERNAL with a template error when a rendered reply does not fit the output type or its metadata is too large. The error's text counts in the entry's bytes, so the call comes before the commit. The HTTP status stays as it is.
- **Candidates.** A gRPC call is matched only against the Mock's gRPC Stubs, Ephemeral ones included, in today's order. An HTTP request never matches a gRPC Stub, so a plain POST to the same path goes to the HTTP Stubs and then `noMatch`.
- **Answered when the HEADERS arrive.** A call is answered UNIMPLEMENTED as soon as its HEADERS arrive, without waiting for its message, when its Host reaches no Mock, its Mock has no set, or its `:path` is not `/service/method` or names no unary method of the set (streaming methods included), unless a built-in service the Mock turns on answers that path. It still goes to the engine, with an empty body, so it is in the Journal as unmatched, with its Near miss when it has one. A call whose Host reaches no Mock, or whose Mock has no gRPC Stub (always so for a Mock without a set), has none, as on HTTP, and its answer carries no `smock-near-miss` trailer. RST_STREAM `NO_ERROR` follows when the request has not ended.
- **The plan.** The engine's response plan gains a gRPC part: the status, the message, the trailers, the details and the reply JSON. A `json` template is escaped as JSON, as today, so a gRPC reply needs no escaping rule of its own.
- **Encoding.** The gRPC layer encodes the reply JSON with the output type and frames it, uncompressed. A static reply was checked at load. A templated one is rendered first; if it does not fit, the call gets INTERNAL and the entry's `templateError` says why.
- **smock's own failures.** smock's own HTTP answers never reach a gRPC call. Each of these is sent as Trailers-Only with `:status` 200 and a fixed ASCII `grpc-message`, and the Journal records its gRPC status:
  - Any template failure of a gRPC Stub (its reply, trailers, details, a `variables` value, or a `dataWrites` key or value) gives INTERNAL `template failed`, with `templateError` as today. UNKNOWN would say the application threw, which a mock's own failure is not.
  - A data write that cannot be applied gives INTERNAL `data write failed`, with `dataError` in the entry.
  - Writes or Variables past the state bound give RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED `state limit reached`, as gRPC lists "out of resources".

### The JSON form

smock's decoded form: what the engine, the Journal and templates see. Replies are read more loosely, below.

| Protobuf | JSON |
|---|---|
| field names | lowerCamelCase, or the field's `json_name`, as ProtoJSON |
| 64-bit integers (int64, uint64, sint64, fixed64, sfixed64) | numbers, exact at any size |
| 32-bit integers, double | numbers, as smock's `json` replies write them |
| float | numbers, in the shortest form that reads back as the same 32-bit float, as protobuf's JSON printers write them, so 0.1f prints `0.1` |
| float, double: special values | `"NaN"`, `"Infinity"` and `"-Infinity"`, as strings |
| bool, string | as JSON |
| bytes | standard base64 with padding |
| enums | the value's name, the first one for an alias; an unknown value of an open enum, its number |
| messages, maps, repeated fields | objects, objects with string keys (integer keys in decimal, bool keys `"true"` and `"false"`), arrays |
| well-known types | ProtoJSON's printed forms: Timestamp in UTC with `Z` and 0, 3, 6 or 9 fractional digits; Duration with 0, 3, 6 or 9 fractional digits, then `s`, such as `"1.500s"`; FieldMask as lowerCamelCase paths joined by commas; Struct, Value, ListValue and the wrappers as their JSON values (Int64Value and UInt64Value as numbers, FloatValue as `float`); Empty as `{}`; Any with `@type` |

- **Presence.** Fields without presence are printed even at their default, so `{"count": 0}` matches. Empty repeated and map fields print `[]` and `{}`. Fields with presence (proto3 `optional`, proto2 fields, messages, oneof members) are printed only when set.
- **Any.** Its type is looked up in the Mock's set. An Any whose type the set lacks cannot be printed, so the call is refused with INTERNAL. An Any holding a well-known type with a special JSON form is `{"@type": …, "value": …}`; one holding Empty is `{"@type": …}` alone.
- **Unknown fields** in a request are skipped.
- **Decoding.** The binary message is read as protobuf's parsers read it. Packed and unpacked repeated scalars are both accepted, and several packed records are joined. For a singular scalar or enum, the last value wins; repeated occurrences of a singular message are merged. A later oneof member replaces an earlier one, so the JSON never holds two. A map entry without a key or a value takes the default; when a key repeats, the last entry wins.
  - A message does not parse when it has a proto3 string that is not UTF-8, field number 0 or one above 2^29-1, wire type 6 or 7, a group end that does not match, or a truncated varint or length.
  - A proto2 string that is not UTF-8 is valid protobuf, but JSON text must be UTF-8: it prints with U+FFFD for each bad sequence, as smock already reads header values.
- **One text per message.** The decoded form is compact, with fields in field-number order, numbers as in the table, and map entries in key order (numbers by value, other keys by their text). So `bodyText`, the Journal and the Near miss show the same text for the same message, whatever order the client encoded it in.
- **Normalised at load.** In a gRPC Stub's conditions and reply, a field may be written with its proto name, and an enum by its number. The loader rewrites both to lowerCamelCase and names, so this costs nothing per request. Templates, `find`, `$each`, Variables and data writes read the decoded body at run time, so they see lowerCamelCase only. Map keys and Struct keys are data, which the name rewrite never touches.
  - An enum alias becomes its first name, as an enum number does.
  - A `float` literal is rounded to the nearest 32-bit float and kept in its printed form, so `{ratio: 0.1}` matches 0.1f. One outside the float range is a load error.
- **Conditions are checked.** Each key must name a field or extension of the type at its place, and each literal must be a value of its type in the form above. So a 64-bit integer written as a string is a load error that suggests the number. Patterns and operators are allowed in any place.
  - Any other exact literal that ProtoJSON reads but never prints is a load error that suggests the printed form: a Duration of `"1.5s"`, a Timestamp with an offset other than `Z`, unpadded or URL-safe base64, an integer map key such as `"007"`. Refusing is simpler than rewriting, and keeps F11's list of normalised spellings short.
- **Replies are read as ProtoJSON.** Either name spelling, enum names or numbers, 64-bit integers as numbers or strings.
  - `null` leaves a field unset, except in a Value or NullValue field, Struct entries included, where it sets `null_value`.
  - These are load errors, or INTERNAL when the reply is templated: `null` inside a repeated field, two members of one oneof, and both spellings of one field in one object.
- **Unknown keys.** An unknown key in a condition or a reply is a load error.

### Metadata

- **Request metadata is headers.** Each field line is one value, as on HTTP. `headers` conditions and `header.NAME` see every field. An exact condition value on a `-bin` field of a gRPC Stub loses its padding at load, in each comma-separated element, so it meets padded and unpadded clients alike. Pattern conditions see the unpadded value.
  - Journal filters see a gRPC call's `-bin` metadata as stored, unpadded, so a filter gives those values unpadded. Filters are not rewritten when parsed: they also meet HTTP entries, whose `-bin` headers are stored as received.
- **Sessions.** The Session is read from `baggage` metadata with the existing `--session-header` and `--session-member`. There is no gRPC-specific key.
- **Reply metadata.** A gRPC Stub's `headers` are the initial metadata; `grpc.trailers` is the trailing metadata.
  - Names starting with `grpc-`, `content-type` and `te` are load errors in both, beside the names smock already refuses. So are `keep-alive`, `proxy-connection` and `upgrade`, which HTTP/2 forbids, and a name that, lower-cased, holds a character other than `0-9`, `a-z`, `_`, `-` and `.`, which gRPC's grammar allows.
  - Several values of one name are an array, as in `headers`.
  - A static value outside 0x20 to 0x7E is a load error. A `-bin` value is written in base64, checked at load, and sent without padding.
  - With `template: true`, trailer values are templates, rendered as header values are, control characters becoming spaces. A rendered `-bin` value that is not base64, or a rendered value outside 0x20 to 0x7E, gives INTERNAL `template failed`, with the reason in `templateError`.

### gRPC Stubs

- **What makes one.** A Stub whose exact `path` names a method of its Mock's set is a gRPC Stub. The method must be unary: a Stub on a client-, server- or bidi-streaming method is a load error that points to R3.
- **Fields.** `scenario`, `variables`, `dataWrites`, `headers` conditions and `template` work as on HTTP.
  - `priority`, weighted `responses` and `fault` work as on HTTP too.
  - `method` may be left out; when given, it must be `POST`.
  - Refused at load: `query`, `cookies`, `form` and `xml` conditions; exact-text and pattern `body` conditions; and `status`, `body`, `bodyFile`, `events` and `llm` (spec G) in a reply. A pre-encoded protobuf body file is left to a later spec.
  - The reply message is `json`, or nothing for an empty message when the status is OK.
  - The Schema drops `required: [status]` on a response; the loader's existing check applies to HTTP Stubs only.
- **Content type.** smock sends `content-type: application/grpc`. A gRPC Stub that gives a Content-Type is a load error, and the loader adds none for its `json` reply.
- **CRUD Stubs** never answer gRPC calls. A CRUD Stub whose path names a method stays an HTTP Stub: it has no request path, so it is never a gRPC Stub.
- **Shadowing.** The warning for a Stub that can never match compares only Stubs of the same kind. A gRPC Stub and an HTTP Stub never shadow each other, CRUD Stubs stay as today among HTTP Stubs, and gRPC Stubs' conditions are compared after the load-time normalisation.
- **Ephemeral Stubs.** gRPC Stubs can be added through the Admin API and are checked against their Mock's set, or refused with 400 `invalid_stub`.
- **A near-method path.** `smock check` warns about a Stub of a Mock with a set whose exact path has the form `/pkg.Service/Method` but names no method of the set.

### Status, message and details

- **`response.grpc`.** A gRPC Stub's reply, or each of its `responses`, may give `grpc` with `status`, `message`, `trailers` and `details`. An HTTP Stub that gives it is refused at load.
- **`status`.** A name from gRPC's seventeen codes, from `OK` to `UNAUTHENTICATED`; `OK` when left out. A gRPC Stub cannot set an HTTP status. The status itself is not templated, as an HTTP status is not.
- **`message`.** Any Unicode text. smock percent-encodes its UTF-8: octets 0x20 to 0x7E other than `%` stay as they are, every other octet becomes `%XX`. A space at either end also becomes `%20`, since HTTP/2 refuses a field value with a space at either end. With `template: true` it is a text template: control characters it renders are kept, then percent-encoded, not turned into spaces as in header values.
- **Metadata size.** The reply's header block and its trailers each count against `--header-size-limit`, as RFC 7541 §4.1 counts them; today the flag bounds request heads only. A static reply over it is a load error, and `smock check` warns above 8 KiB, the limit gRPC says a client may set. A rendered reply over the flag, or over the SETTINGS_MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE the client advertised, is replaced by Trailers-Only INTERNAL with the fixed message `reply metadata too large`, and `templateError` says why. Both blocks are known before anything is sent, so the swap is always possible.
- **`details`.** Each element is ProtoJSON with `@type`. Its type is looked up in the Mock's set; a missing type is a load error. smock builds `google.rpc.Status` from the status, the message and the details packed as Any, and sends it as `grpc-status-details-bin`, in base64 without padding. So the codes never disagree, and the set need not hold `google/rpc/status.proto`.
  - Details with status `OK` are a load error, since gRPC allows them only on an error. With `template: true`, details are structured templates, rendered then encoded.
- **Error replies carry no message.** A gRPC Stub whose status is not OK and that also gives `json` is a load error: a unary client receives a message or an error, never both.

### The reply on the wire

- **OK.** HEADERS with `:status` 200, `content-type`, `smock-mock` when the Default Mock answered, and the initial metadata; one DATA message, flag 0; then HEADERS that end the stream, with `grpc-status: 0` and the trailing metadata.
- **Errors.** With initial metadata: HEADERS, then the trailers. Without: Trailers-Only, one HEADERS block that ends the stream, with `:status` 200, `content-type`, `grpc-status`, `grpc-message` when given, `grpc-status-details-bin` when there are details, smock's own fields and the trailing metadata. smock's own fields (`smock-mock`, `smock-near-miss`) do not count as initial metadata for this rule.
- **`:status`** is 200 on every answer except the protocol refusals of the table below: 405 for a method other than POST and 400 for a malformed `grpc-timeout`.
- **No `content-length` and no `grpc-encoding`** on gRPC replies, the `partial` Fault's HEADERS included.
- **After the trailers,** RST_STREAM `NO_ERROR` when the client's side of the stream is still open, as grpc-go does.
- Spec E's rules for HTTP/2 responses apply to initial metadata, trailers and smock's own fields alike: lower-case names, the fields HTTP/2 forbids left out, and spaces or tabs around a value trimmed.

### Unmatched calls

- **UNIMPLEMENTED.** An unmatched call gets UNIMPLEMENTED with a fixed ASCII `grpc-message`, `no Stub matched`, as Trailers-Only.
- **The Near miss** goes in a `smock-near-miss` trailer, in the form of the HTTP `Smock-Near-Miss` header: ASCII, percent-encoded names, never what a condition expects or what the call sent. The Journal records the full Near miss, and the unmatched list includes the call.
- **Calls answered from their HEADERS** get fixed messages too: `no Mock for this Host`, `the Mock has no Descriptor set`, `unknown method` and `streaming methods are not served yet`.
- **`noMatch`** applies to HTTP requests only. Its status and headers never reach a gRPC call.

### Protocol checks

None of these reaches the engine. Like spec E's refused streams, they count as rejected traffic with `mock=""` and `stub=""`, and are not in the Journal. A refusal sent before the request has ended is followed by RST_STREAM `NO_ERROR`.

| Request | Checked | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| A method other than POST | on HEADERS | `:status` 405, INTERNAL |
| A malformed `grpc-timeout` (not 1 to 8 digits and one of `H M S m u n`) | on HEADERS | `:status` 400, INTERNAL |
| An unsupported subtype, such as `+json` | on HEADERS | UNIMPLEMENTED |
| No `te: trailers` | never | served |
| A body over `--body-limit`, prefix included, by `content-length`, by the message length or by the octets received | as soon as it shows | RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, at once, instead of spec E's 413 |
| A flag byte other than 0 or 1, or flag 1 without a `grpc-encoding` other than `identity` | on the prefix | INTERNAL |
| Flag 1 with such a `grpc-encoding` (F5) | on the prefix | UNIMPLEMENTED, `grpc-accept-encoding: identity` |
| The request ends inside a prefix or a message | at the end of the request | INTERNAL |
| No message, or several | at the end | UNIMPLEMENTED |
| A message that does not parse, nests deeper than 100, or lacks a proto2 required field | at the end | INTERNAL |
| Decoded JSON over `--body-limit` | while printing | RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED |

- **The order on HEADERS.** Spec E's checks, then `:method`, the subtype and `grpc-timeout`, then the Mock, its set and the method. The first that fails gives the answer.
- **A zero-length message**, `00 00 00 00 00`, is one message, decoded with every field at its default. So a call taking `Empty`, or health `Check` for `""`, is served.
- **Decoder limits.** Nesting depth is capped at 100, the default of protobuf's C++ and Java parsers. Every length is checked against the bytes left and the body limit before anything is allocated. The decoded JSON is counted while it is printed: printing fields at their defaults lets a 2-byte empty element of a repeated message print every field of its type, so a 10 MiB message could otherwise print gigabytes. The cap makes a gRPC call cost no more than the largest JSON body an HTTP request may send. Each limit is tested beside spec E's denial-of-service cases.
- **No `te` check.** grpc-go never checks it; a mock should accept every real client.

### Deadlines

- **`grpc-timeout`** is read from the HEADERS, and the deadline counts from their arrival. Without it, a call has no deadline.
- **Large and zero values.** The value converts with saturation, so eight digits of hours never wrap. A deadline beyond the longest delay smock can give (2^31-1 ms) acts as no deadline. A value of 0 in any unit is accepted: its deadline is the arrival, so any delay ends at once with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, and a call without a delay is served.
- **A delay that outlasts it.** When a Stub's delay would end after the deadline, the call ends at the deadline with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, as Trailers-Only, with the fixed message `deadline exceeded`. The Journal entry is committed then, with gRPC status DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, set by the entry's final-status method, and HTTP status 200. Scenario moves, Variables and data writes stand, as they stand after any delay.
- **A client that resets at its deadline.** Clients that enforce deadlines, such as grpc-go, grpc-java and grpcurl's `-max-time`, reset the stream with `CANCEL` at their own deadline. `grpc-timeout` carries the time left when the HEADERS were built, so smock's deadline trails the client's by about one transit. A client reset that arrives while a delay runs past the deadline, at or after that deadline less a fixed tolerance of 100 ms, ends the entry as DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, as if smock's timer had fired. So the entry does not depend on which comes first.
- **Spec E's defences (FX1).** A client reset that the rule above turns into DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, or that lands on a stream smock has ended with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, counts neither toward the Rapid Reset bound nor among the frames that do no work. This holds once per stream: a second reset of the stream, and any other reset of a gRPC call, count as spec E's E3 says, and E3 lists this exception. smock keeps the IDs of the streams it ended with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED until their resets arrive, at most `--http2-max-concurrent-streams` per connection, the oldest dropped first.
- **Only the delay.** smock watches the deadline only while a delay runs. Once the reply's HEADERS are out, the reply finishes as planned.
- **No new timer.** The delay already gives the stream a task (spec E); that task sleeps until the earlier of the two.

### Compression

- **Never decompressed.** A message with flag 1 under a `grpc-encoding` other than `identity` gets UNIMPLEMENTED with `grpc-accept-encoding: identity`, as gRPC's compression rules prescribe. Its message names the encoding received, percent-encoded, and `identity`, as those rules require. Flag 1 otherwise is INTERNAL. A message with flag 0 is served whatever `grpc-encoding` says.
- **Replies are never compressed.** smock has no decompressor and no compressor, so there is no compression-bomb surface.

### Faults

Spec E's per-stream forms apply, unchanged except that no `content-length` is sent. The engine decides Faults as today, with the same draws and seeds.

| Fault | On a gRPC call | The client sees |
|---|---|---|
| delay | Waits before the reply's HEADERS; the deadline can cut it short. | The reply, later; or DEADLINE_EXCEEDED |
| `reset` | RST_STREAM `INTERNAL_ERROR` on the call's stream only. | INTERNAL |
| `partial` | The reply's HEADERS and the first half of the framed message's octets, rounded down, then RST_STREAM `INTERNAL_ERROR`. A reply with no message sends its HEADERS without the status fields and without ending the stream, then the reset. | INTERNAL |
| `close` | GOAWAY, then the connection closes. Every call in flight on the connection ends with it, which the docs warn about: gRPC clients multiplex calls on one connection. | UNAVAILABLE |

- **Probabilistic gRPC errors** are weighted `responses` with a `grpc` status, not a new Fault kind.
- **Spec E's own resets.** The guide also gives the status a client derives from spec E's resets and refusals: REFUSED_STREAM past the stream limit gives UNAVAILABLE, which gRPC retries transparently; the read timeout and a stream held at a zero window give CANCELLED; a header list over twice the limit gives RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED; 431 gives UNKNOWN and 400 gives INTERNAL. After a defence's GOAWAY, calls in flight end and later calls get UNAVAILABLE.
- **The Journal.** An entry ended by `reset` or `close` has no status and no gRPC status; a `partial` one keeps both, as spec E keeps the status.

### Keepalive, idle channels and the drain

- **PINGs.** Client PINGs are answered under spec E's limits on frames that do no work, which already follow gRPC's rule for PINGs sent while data flows. There is no separate gRPC ping-strike policy.
- **Idle channels.** An HTTP/2 connection with no open stream gets GOAWAY after `--idle-timeout-ms`, PINGs or not (spec E). A gRPC client reconnects on its next call; the guide says so.
- **The drain.** On SIGTERM, spec E's two-step GOAWAY applies: calls opened after it see UNAVAILABLE and are retried elsewhere, as gRPC's "server shutting down" is UNAVAILABLE, and calls in flight finish within the drain timeout. Health turns NOT_SERVING at the same moment.

### Built-in services

- **Per Mock, off by default.** `grpc.reflection` and `grpc.health` turn them on. A Mock that does not turn them on pays nothing.
- **Reflection.** `grpc.reflection.v1` and `v1alpha`. It is a bidirectional-streaming method, so smock answers one request per call: it reads the first request message, sends one response message and the OK trailers, then RST_STREAM `NO_ERROR` if the client's side is still open. MockServer answers reflection this way by default.
  - It answers from the Mock's set: `list_services` with its services; `file_by_filename`, `file_containing_symbol` and `file_containing_extension` with the file and its dependencies, each without SourceCodeInfo; `all_extension_numbers_of_type`. A symbol is any named element: a message, nested type, field, enum, enum value, service, method or extension. Each response echoes `original_request` and sets `valid_host` to the call's Host. A name the set lacks gets the reflection `error_response` with NOT_FOUND.
- **Health.** `grpc.health.v1.Health/Check` answers SERVING for `""` and for each service in the Mock's set, NOT_FOUND for other names, and NOT_SERVING for all once SIGTERM starts the drain. `List` returns the same statuses. `Watch` is server streaming and gets UNIMPLEMENTED until R3.
- **A Stub wins.** When the Mock has a Stub on the path, an Ephemeral one of the call's Session included, the call goes to the Stubs. A Stub there needs the service's `.proto` in the set, like any gRPC Stub.
- **Not journaled.** Health and reflection answers are counted in the request metrics under their Mock with an empty `stub` label, not as unmatched requests, and are not recorded in the Journal. Probes every few seconds and reflection's round trips would otherwise evict the calls tests verify. A reserved `stub` value would not do: it could collide with a Stub ID, as `ephemeral` can today.
- **Their messages.** smock encodes the health and reflection messages itself. A descriptor of gRPC's `health.proto` is embedded in smock, with a NOTICE entry (Apache-2.0). On a Mock with `health` on, reflection lists `grpc.health.v1.Health` and answers its file from that descriptor, so grpcurl finds the health service without the user adding `health.proto` to the set (FX4). When the Mock's set defines `grpc.health.v1` itself, reflection answers from the set.
- **smock's own probes** stay on the admin port's `/readyz`. A call whose `:authority` reaches no Mock, such as a Pod IP with no Default Mock, gets UNIMPLEMENTED like any call.
